       Notice of Ofwat’s proposal to issue an enforcement order and impose a penalty
                               on South East Water Limited



About this document
This document constitutes a notice under sections 20 and 22A(4) of the Water Industry
Act 1991 (WIA91). It sets out our proposal to issue an enforcement order to South East
Water Limited (South East Water) as a result of its contraventions of section 37 of the
WIA91 and Condition P12 of its instrument of appointment (Licence). It also sets out our
proposed decision to impose a financial penalty on South East Water. It is accompanied
by the proposed enforcement order, requiring it to remedy the contraventions that we
have identified.

The document summarises the evidence that we have gathered and sets out our
findings in relation to the issues under investigation, including why we believe that
South East Water has contravened its statutory duty and the obligations of its Licence.

Interested parties are invited to comment on our proposed decision and the proposed
enforcement order. We will take representations received into account before making a
final decision on whether to issue an enforcement order and the terms of that
enforcement order, as well as whether to impose a penalty and the level of that
penalty.




                                           2
       Notice of Ofwat’s proposal to issue an enforcement order and impose a penalty
                               on South East Water Limited



Executive Summary
This notice describes our ﬁndings of contraventions by South East Water and how these
have occurred. The investigation was opened due to South East Water's continued poor
performance regarding water supply interruptions and several major loss of supply
events since 2018 in its Kent and Sussex regions (referred to as its Eastern region).
Whilst South East Water considered that the root cause of these events was due to
extreme weather, we have found that they were in part attributable to and/or
exacerbated by failures by South East Water itself to develop and maintain an efﬁcient
water supply system and meet its general duty under section 37 WIA91 to act in a
manner which is best calculated to ensure that it has in place adequate resources and
systems of planning and control to enable it to carry out its functions as required by
Licence Condition P12. In the course of this investigation we uncovered fundamental
issues with South East Water's basic maintenance of assets and systems planning as
well as a failure to plan for extreme weather.

Throughout our investigation we made detailed requests for, and obtained, information
and data from South East Water.

Having reviewed this information, we have identiﬁed that:


     •   South East Water has failed to maintain key assets including its boreholes,
         service reservoirs and trunk mains which meant that its asset base in the
         Eastern region was not sufficiently resilient to adequately perform when
         demand increased. Further, it failed to have adequate proactive maintenance
         plans and to increase storage levels at service reservoirs in the lead up to
         critical periods.
     •   Regarding its systems planning, we found that South East Water failed to
         manage its supply demand balance and headroom which resulted in the
         company being with less headroom and less able to respond than we would
         expect a reasonable company to have be able to in the lead up to, and during
         periods of high demand. This included failing to effectively use planning tools
         available to it (such as area plans, peak week production capacity (PWPC), up-
         to-date hydraulic models, root cause analysis) and to mitigate known risks
         posed by extreme weather and climate change.
     •   This has had a detrimental effect on South East Water's customers. Compared
         to its Western region and other companies in the south east of England, South
         East Water's Eastern region has been disproportionately affected by supply
         interruption incidents since 2020 which were attributable to and/or
         exacerbated by these failures of South East Water. These events affected a
         total of 286,645 customers, with some customers being affected by repeat
         incidents. Our investigation makes no ﬁndings with respect to the Western


                                            3
        Notice of Ofwat’s proposal to issue an enforcement order and impose a penalty
                                on South East Water Limited



          region (which was not covered by this investigation). To the extent that
          speciﬁc actions by South East Water are company-wide, we ﬁnd that it has
          failed to take appropriate action with respect to the vulnerabilities that existed
          and were known in its Eastern region.
      •   Further, South East Water's operational response to incidents has been poor, it
          had insufﬁcient incident and emergency response, particularly with respect to
          availability of bottled water, mutual aid, tankers and for the support for
          vulnerable sites within its emergency plan. In general, we observed a failure
          by South East Water to learn relevant lessons from past incidents and
          implement actions identiﬁed following those incidents.
      •   The relevant period for this investigation is from 15 November 2018 and
          remains ongoing (the Relevant Period). However, given that our investigation
          was at an advanced stage during the recent supply interruption issues in
          Sussex and Kent in November 2025 to January 2026, we have not obtained
          evidence in relation to those incidents or examined them as part of this
          enforcement case. Ofwat has opened a separate investigation regarding these
          incidents to consider whether it has complied with its obligation to provide
          high standards of customer service and support for its customers under
          Licence Condition G. 1

We consider that our analysis of the evidence we have gathered, at this stage,
demonstrates that South East Water has failed to meet the following duties and
obligations:


      •   To develop and maintain an efﬁcient and economical system of water supply
          within its area and to ensure all such arrangements are made for providing
          supplies of water to premises in that area and for making such supplies
          available to persons who demand them and for maintaining, improving and
          extending water mains and other pipes, under section 37 WIA91; and
      •   To, at all times, act in a manner which is best calculated to ensure that it has
          in place adequate ﬁnancial resources and facilities, management resources
          and systems of planning and internal control, under Licence Condition P12.

Based on the evidence provided to us, in relation to section 37 WIA91, we are satisﬁed
that, during the Relevant Period, South East Water has breached and continues to be in
breach of its duty by:




1
  This investigation does not cover Licence Condition G (the customer-focused licence condition which
requires companies to comply with the principles of customer care) because it was not in force and cannot
apply to incidents prior to February 2024.

                                                   4
 Notice of Ofwat’s proposal to issue an enforcement order and impose a penalty
                         on South East Water Limited



•   Failing to develop and maintain an efﬁcient and economical system of water
    supply within its Eastern region and, separately, to ensure all such
    arrangements have been made for providing water supply to meet demand, as
    is necessary for securing its obligations under Part III, speciﬁcally:
    • Failings in maintenance of key assets including its inspection and
        maintenance of service reservoirs and boreholes, which reduced supply
        resilience. South East Water did not maintain adequate storage levels in
        advance of and during critical periods. Its general approach to
        maintenance was reactive instead of proactive and failed to adequately
        plan for critical or high demand periods or assess system-wide risks.
    • Failings in planning for its water resources within its water supply system
        at a sub-zonal level. South East Water failed to manage its supply demand
        balance and headroom at a sub-zonal level which resulted in the company
        being with less headroom and less able to respond than we would expect a
        reasonable company to have be able to in the lead up to, and during the
        Events in the Relevant Period. Sub-zonal planning is particularly important
        for South East Water's Eastern region because some sub-zonal areas lack
        interconnectivity and have single points of failure. This included failing to
        mitigate known risks posed by extreme weather and climate change,
        including implementing the actions and recommendations from the
        Drinking Water Inspectorate (DWI)'s and Ofwat's review of the 2018 Freeze
        Thaw Event.
    • Failings in its operational response to supply interruptions. South East
        Water failed to maintain a sufficient operational response to supply
        interruption incidents leaving customers at risk of being unduly without
        water during peak periods. In particular:
         • Failure to respond promptly at the start of incidents, using all available
             operational tools.
         • Failure to deploy alternative water supplies effectively, including
             bottled water, tankers, and mutual aid arrangements.
         • Failure to plan for and prioritise vulnerable sites to ensure support
             reached those most at risk within its emergency plan.
•   Failure to develop and maintain an efﬁcient and economical system of water
    supply within its Eastern region and, separately, to ensure all such
    arrangements have been made for maintaining, improving and extending its
    water mains and other pipes, as is necessary for securing its obligations under
    Part III, speciﬁcally:
    • Failings in the preventative maintenance of trunk mains. South East
        Water relied disproportionately on reactive maintenance and did not
        undertake sufficient preventative maintenance or renewal of its trunk
        mains. These assets were a contributing factor to supply interruptions in
        the Eastern region.

                                       5
       Notice of Ofwat’s proposal to issue an enforcement order and impose a penalty
                               on South East Water Limited



Based on the evidence provided to us, in relation to Licence Condition P12 these failures
to comply were caused by the company:


     •   Failing to establish and implement effective programmes for the routine
         inspection and maintenance of key assets. In particular, failure to use
         internal targets and plans to conduct proactive programmes to carry out
         regular inspections and maintenance at service reservoirs, maintain trunk
         mains and optimise borehole yield; failure to maintain adequate storage levels
         at reservoirs during peak periods and failure to plan maintenance activities
         with sufﬁcient regard to peak demand and system-wide risk.
     •   Failing to use the planning tools available to it such as its area plans, PWPC,
         up-to-date hydraulic models, root cause analysis and to mitigate known risks
         posed by extreme weather and climate change, including implementing the
         actions and recommendations from the DWI's and Ofwat's review of the 2018
         Freeze Thaw Event.
     •   Failing in its preparedness and resilience for supply interruptions. South East
         Water failed to adequately plan for and manage supply interruptions, including
         establishing what support is required for vulnerable sites and reﬂecting this in
         its emergency plan, mitigating known risks, ensuring operational staff had the
         right information and controls, maintaining alternative water supply
         arrangements, and deploying sufﬁcient resources to prevent customers being
         unduly without water during peak periods.
     •   Failings in Executive and Board level oversight and assurance. South East
         Water’s Executive Team and Board did not ensure that adequate reporting
         metrics and management information were in place to provide a clear and
         accurate understanding of the company’s compliance with its general duty
         under section 37 WIA91. In addition, it failed to effectively monitor and
         challenge risks to supply system resilience, to properly scrutinise compliance
         with legal and regulatory obligations, and ensure that timely and appropriate
         action was taken to in response to those risks.

In response to our information request issued when we opened the investigation, in
November 2023, South East Water has developed an action plan to address short-term
supply system resilience issues, which also refers to the resilience schemes identiﬁed
in the price review process for 2025-30 (Action Plan). Notwithstanding the steps that
South East Water is now beginning to take, Ofwat considers that there remain
signiﬁcant additional measures that the company needs to take to become compliant
with its legal and regulatory obligations. We also consider that the contraventions that
have taken place are sufﬁciently serious to warrant the imposition of a penalty of
£22.46m in this case. Ofwat therefore proposes to require South East Water to:



                                            6
       Notice of Ofwat’s proposal to issue an enforcement order and impose a penalty
                               on South East Water Limited



a) Obtain a report from an independent third party reviewer (approved by Ofwat)
   examining its approach to:
    (i) Review its root cause analysis process and approach to identify the underlying
        causes of failings to comply with section 37 WIA91 including maintenance,
         planning and operational response;
    (ii) Review its incident management procedures, including operational tools and
        escalation triggers; deployment of alternative water supplies and
        implementing lessons learnt from previous incidents.
    (iii)    Review the scope of the company's root-and-branch review of hydraulic
         models;
    (iv) Conduct a root cause analysis of the failings identiﬁed in this decision;
    (v) Make recommendations for remediating the failings, taking into account
           deliverability, affordability and ﬁnanceability.
b) Prepare a remediation plan (for approval by Ofwat), applying the recommendations
   from the independent reviews, setting out the further actions it needs to undertake
   to demonstrate how it will invest in and maintain resilience within its water supply
   system to minimise the risk of supply interruptions to its customers.
c) In line with our ﬁndings in this draft decision, we also require South East Water to
   undertake the following actions:
     (i) Conduct a root-and-branch review of all its hydraulic models.
     (ii) Establish what support is required for vulnerable sites and including this within
          its emergency plan.
     (iii)       Conduct a thorough lessons learnt, including root cause analysis, one
          month after each water supply interruption incident in the future.
d) Prepare (and report to Ofwat) on a management plan to ensure its senior
   management and Board actively review and challenge compliance with its general
   duty under section 37 WIA91 and the Security and Emergency Measures Direction.




                                            7
        Notice of Ofwat’s proposal to issue an enforcement order and impose a penalty
                                on South East Water Limited




1. Introduction
1.1.   This document constitutes a notice issued by the Water Services Regulation
       Authority (Ofwat) to inform South East Water that it proposes to issue an
       enforcement order under section 18 WIA91 and impose on it a penalty under
       sections 22A(1) and (2) WIA91.

1.2.   The proposed enforcement order and penalty relate to South East Water:

        •   Contravening its duty under section 37 WIA91 by not maintaining an efficient
            and economical system of water supply within its area and not ensuring that
            all such arrangements were made for providing supplies of water to
            premises in that area and maintaining, improving and extending water
            mains and other pipes.

        •   Contravening Licence Condition P12 in relation to acting in the manner best
            calculated to ensure that it has in place adequate financial resources and
            facilities, management resources and systems of planning and internal
            control to meet its duties under section 37 WIA91 and the Security and
            Emergency Measures Direction (SEMD).

1.3.   Ofwat considers that a penalty of £22.46m is appropriate.

1.4.   As required by sections 20 and 22A(4) WIA91, we provide more details of the
       proposed enforcement order and financial penalty referenced above, together
       with details of the contraventions to which they relate, in Sections 2 to 6 of this
       notice. This notice is structured as follows:
       • Section 2 sets out some relevant background on the operation the water
           industry and the relevant legislative framework;
       • Section 3 explains the nature of our investigation, summarises the evidence
           we have considered and sets out our assessment of this evidence;
       • Section 4 sets out our findings in relation to contraventions;
       • Section 5 outlines our proposal to issue an enforcement order in this case;
       • Section 6 details the facts which we consider justify our decision to impose
           a financial penalty, and the amount of that penalty.

1.5.   Under sections 20(1)(c) and 22A(4)(d) WIA91, this notice must allow at least
       21 days for representations on or objections to our proposal to be made. We
       explain how to make representations about or objections to this notice in
       Section 7.



                                            8
        Notice of Ofwat’s proposal to issue an enforcement order and impose a penalty
                                on South East Water Limited




2. Relevant background
2.1.    Section 2 provides background information on the provision, operation and
        maintenance of typical water treatment works and a water company's supply
        system; the relevant legislative framework for our investigation; and our
        approach to enforcement of the relevant provisions.



2.1 The water supply system
The subsections below provide details of relevant components of the water supply
system referred to in this investigation.

2.1.1 Water only companies
2.2.    Water only companies, such as South East Water, provide water by collecting,
        storing and treating it to high standards so it can be distributed to homes and
        businesses via a network of pipes. 2

2.1.2 Boreholes
2.3.    Boreholes are shafts bored into the ground that are used to extract groundwater
        via a pump, or to monitor and/or measure water quality and/or quantity. 3


2.4.    The maintenance of boreholes is extremely important as it ensures the lifespan
        of the borehole and maintains its efﬁciency and yield. If a borehole is not
        maintained, its efﬁciency will decrease and will eventually no longer be able to
        supply raw water. This leads to the need for boreholes to be replaced earlier
        than the estimated life of the asset.

2.1.3 Water treatment works
2.5.    Water treatment works (WTWs) are treatment plants where raw water is cleaned
        and ﬁltered. The water is then disinfected to ensure water borne diseases are
        eliminated and the pH level is adjusted if the water is too acidic or alkaline.
        Following the ﬁnal treatment, the water leaves the treatment works and is
        stored in covered service reservoirs where it is pumped to customers through a
        network of mains and pumping stations.




2
  Water and sewerage companies also deliver this function, but they also take used water and waste away
to treat it so that it can be discharged back to the environment (e.g. into rivers or the sea).
3
  Environment Agency, Borehole

         Notice of Ofwat’s proposal to issue an enforcement order and impose a penalty
                                 on South East Water Limited



2.1.4 Service reservoirs
2.6.    Service reservoirs are a vital asset for the continuous provision of water to
        customers by providing storage of treated potable water. This storage helps
        companies to respond to changes in demand from customers. As a key part of
        the water supply infrastructure, a regular programme of reservoir inspection,
        cleaning and maintenance is required to reduce the potential for
        microbiological, chemical or physical problems from service reservoirs. 4


2.7.    If service reservoirs are not regularly inspected and cleaned, it is possible that
        when a clean and inspection does eventually take place, several issues could be
        identiﬁed with drinking water quality and/or the structural integrity of the
        service reservoir. If this is the case, this may result in having to take service
        reservoirs out of use for extended periods of time to carry out remedial works.
        This impacts the amount of water available for a speciﬁc region or resource zone
        unexpectedly which, in the event of a supply demand incident, increases the
        risk of customers experiencing supply interruptions.


2.8.    In England, service reservoirs that are capable of holding 25,000m³ or more of
        water are regulated under the Reservoirs Act 1975. The undertakers (owners or
        operators) of these reservoirs are required to register them with the
        Environment Agency following which the reservoirs are designated as "high risk"
        or "not high risk". Those designated high risk are subject to inspection and
        service by reservoir engineers. Those designated not high risk are not subject to
        the same degree of inspection and supervision.


2.9.    High risk reservoirs that fall within the Reservoirs Act 1975 must be inspected
        every ten years. 5 According to UK Water Industry Research (UKWIR) 6 the
        targeted inspection interval should reﬂect the strategic importance of perceived




4

5
  Section 10(2) of the Reservoirs Act 1975 states that "[u]nless it is at the time under the supervision of a
construction engineer (…) a high-risk reservoir must be inspected under this section at the time specified
by regulations made by the Minister." Regulation 6 of The Reservoirs Act 1975 (Exemptions, Appeals and
Inspections) (England) Regulations 2013 sets out the requirements for periodical inspections of high-risk
reservoirs. Depending on the circumstances, the next inspection is due within 6 months, 2 years, 10 years
or at any time recommended by the supervising engineer or inspecting engineer. The 10-year period is a
stand-alone requirement and is not an alternative to the other requirements. Therefore, there are no
circumstances in which a high-risk reservoir may be inspected more than 10 years after the date of the
previous inspection. The Environment Agency has a duty to enforce the 10-year maximum period between
high-risk reservoir inspections.
6

        level of risk of the individual service reservoirs.7 Most water companies have
        standard inspection frequencies (linked to cleaning and maintenance) of
        between one and ten years. Some have a risked-based approach as assets age
        or problems arise e.g. inspect on a ﬁve-yearly rolling programme but increase to
        three-yearly when considered high risk, for instance, if a service reservoir is a
        single point of failure or its loss would lead to a supply interruption. 8 According
        to a 2015 joint publication by the DWI, Water UK 9 and Royal Society for Public
        Health, in addition to the requirements of the Reservoirs Act 1975, it is good
        practice that internal inspection should be carried out at a frequency of not
        greater than every ten years. 10


2.10.   As service reservoirs are an important asset in the provision of good quality and
        reliable water sources, it is imperative that storage levels are at the highest
        capacity as possible. According to the UKWIR, the normal operational volume of
        a service reservoir should consider the sum of diurnal storage, which is the daily
        variation between generally constant water production and constantly varying
        consumer demand, and strategic storage, which is the stored water reserves
        needed to meet consumer demands in the event of unplanned interruptions to
        water supply or emergency storage. 11 The normal operational volume of a service
        reservoir should also consider operating top water level to overﬂow depth, ﬂood
        depth, freeboard depth, anti-vortex depth, and washout volume. 12 UKWIR
        demonstrates this explanation by using a hypothetical service reservoir to
        demonstrate with a full operating range of 1974m3; however, the service
        reservoir's normal operating range would be 1680m3, of which 1274m3 would
        represent strategic storage. 13 This means that a service reservoir's normal
        operation volume would be 80-85% of the total volume of the service reservoir.
        As such, we consider an 80-85% target should be the standard target year-

2.1.5 Booster pumps
2.11.    Booster pumps are used to help distribute water to customers on higher ground.
         They increase the pressure in water supply systems, particularly in areas with
         low pressure or during peak demand times.

2.1.6 Mains
2.12.    There are three different types of water pipe in a company's network. Water
         mains, which are the large company pipes that distribute water around the
         network. There are then two types of water pipes that transmit supply from
         water mains to customers: the communication pipes (which carry water from
         the company water mains and the boundary of private property) and the supply
         pipes (which carry water from company water mains onto private property).15

2.13.    Trunk mains are a subset of water mains and are pipelines that are generally laid
         with a depth cover of 900mm below the ground surface, conveying water in bulk
         between a reservoir, treatment works or pumping station and a service reservoir
         or a distribution network of pipes. Trunk mains are among the most critical
         assets operated by the water industry: a catastrophic failure of a trunk main
         could be hugely destructive and leave many customers without water. 16 As these
         are such critical assets, regular trunk mains investigations and leakage surveys
         ensure efﬁciency and reliability of these assets to reduce the risk of failure. 17


2.14.    Water company pipes are susceptible during winter to a period at or below
         freezing temperatures, followed by rapid thaws, that can cause signiﬁcant burst
         pipes and leaks that result in supply interruptions. These are referred to as
         Freeze Thaw events. 18




14

demand changes. For example, demand may be highest in the morning when people are showering. As
such, storage levels are typically at higher levels ready for the peak demand.

2.15.   Ofwat assesses the health of companies' assets and considers their mains
        repairs and unplanned outage performance over the course of a year in the
        annual Water Company Performance Report. It is critical that water companies
        have assets, including trunk mains, that are well maintained and operate as
        intended so that they meet the requirements of their statutory obligations and
        the needs of customers, the environment and wider society. The maintenance of
        trunk mains should include both proactive and reactive maintenance.


2.16.   In order to address the issue of aging assets, water companies will generally
        replace or renew those assets. Mains replacement is generally considered
        preventative maintenance and is one of the ways companies can improve the
        resilience of their water supply systems. According to a UKWIR research paper
        entitled 'Trunk Mains Preventative Maintenance to Reduce Major Incident Risk,
        2020/21', many water companies have recognised the beneﬁts from trunk main
        preventative maintenance and have programmes in place to replace mains.

2.1.7 Valves
2.17.   Valves play an integral role in a water distribution system as they are responsible
        for regulating water ﬂow, maintaining pressure, opening and closing water ﬂow.
        The operation of valves can be used to redirect ﬂows through the network, for
        example to maintain or restore supplies to customers in response to incidents
        such as bursts. They can either be operated manually or can be automated.

2.18.   UKWIR states that a failure to maintain valves increases the risk of supply
        interruptions and creates water quality problems. 19

2.1.8 Preventative maintenance
2.19.   An asset management focused utility should operate an effective asset
        management system that allows it to make informed risk based decisions. As
        part of this system it will have an up-to-date asset maintenance strategy that is
        designed to ensure assets are maintained, repaired or renewed to deliver the
        expected levels of service to the wider system. This will include making informed
        decisions regarding the balance of proactive (preventative) and reactive
        (corrective) maintenance activities linked back to the probability and likelihood
        of failure and its consequence in delivering the desired service. Assets should be
        maintained in line with documented policy to reduce the likelihood of failure
        and operated in accordance with the expected level of service. One way to do



19

22/WM/08/75.

                                                 13
         Notice of Ofwat’s proposal to issue an enforcement order and impose a penalty

        this is to operate and maintain the asset according to the manufacturers’
        recommendations and known wear and tear in the local system. Preventative
        maintenance is often recommended at certain intervals by the manufacturer
        and adjusted based on known conditions. Preventative maintenance usually
        extends the useful life of an asset, lowering its cost of ownership and reduces
        risk of failure. It is also less expensive than reactive maintenance as companies
        can plan for peak times, reducing labour costs and customer impacts.

2.1.9 Supply/demand balance
2.20. Maintaining the balance between water supply and demand is important for
      water supply resilience and for meeting a water company's duty to maintain an
        economic and efﬁcient water supply system. Supply demand planning is
        undertaken at water resource zone (WRZ) level in a water resources
        management plan (WRMP). A WRZ describes an area within which the sources
        of water and distribution of water to meet demand, is largely self-contained
        (apart from any agreed bulk transfers). However, it is also important to consider
        whether there is sufﬁcient supply resilience at the sub-zonal level (i.e. within
        each WRZ) requiring appropriate interconnectivity and resilient supplies within
        the WRZ to ensure resource can be shared between customers within the zone
        and hence all and customers will experience approximately the same risk of
        supply failure. 20


2.21.   Two key metrics used in water resource planning are deployable output and
        distribution input. Deployable output (DO) is the reliable output of a source (or
        groupings / all sources across a water resource zone). It is constrained by
        factors such as the environment, licences, treatment or network constraints and
        water quality. Distribution input (DI) is a measure of demand based on the
        amount of potable water that enters the distribution system (from a WTW site, or
        sites across a WRZ) to downstream networks.


2.22.   Companies must retain headroom to ensure a secure and reliable water supply.
        Headroom is the difference between total water available for use (WAFU) and
        the volume of DI to meet demand. For instance, the difference between the
        amount of water a company has available to supply and the volume of water it
        expects to introduce into its network to meet demand. Target headroom is the
        amount of headroom that a company has set out in its WRMP, over its planning
        horizon, based on how much it thinks it will need as a buffer to cover future

2.23.   The unplanned outage performance commitment (PC) incentivises good asset
        health. This measure should be used as a means of assessing asset health

        abstraction and water treatment activities. As part of calculating their
        unplanned outage PC, since the 2019 price review (PR19), companies are

        peak is important to understand and measure and use as a planning tool.


2.24.   Ofwat's unplanned outage PC guidance states: "PWPC is equivalent to the
        maximum volume of water which can be put into supply and sustained over a
        period of one week measured in megalitres per day (Ml/d). This should be at
        least as great as the highest historic performance that has been sustained for
        any seven-day period in the last ﬁve years (unless a change to assets or process
        can be evidenced) but could be higher. This should be supported by physical
        tests to demonstrate capability undertaken at least once every ﬁve years. It is
        expected that this value should be reviewed annually and periodically as
        modiﬁcations to assets and processes are completed which impact capacity." 21
        The guidance explains in further detail that these ﬁve yearly tests should
        evidence actual output or capacity and be based on a risk-based approach for

        guidance also explicitly states that PWPC does not account for seasonal changes
        in yield (most commonly observed at groundwater sources) and allowed
        abstraction volumes (most commonly observed at river sources) which are
        weather dependent and not an indicator of asset health.23

2.1.10 Hydraulic modelling
2.27.   Hydraulic models illustrate effects of changing demand and climatic conditions
        on water distribution systems – as such modelling is a key element of identifying
        areas of supply risk under current and future scenarios, predicting pressures
        and identifying bottlenecks. It also plays a role in demonstrating the
        effectiveness of proposed solutions to reduce these risks.27 This is essential for
        optioneering processes, including in demonstrating optimal solutions for
        considerations in the water resource management planning and price review

        investments. 29 It assists in both day-to-day operations and future planning by

        potential concerns, and identifying areas that may become overloaded in the

        for optimum, real-time decision-making during an incident or event. 31

      approach that adopts a proactive, rather than reactive, management of issues
           by preventing recurring issues. RCA is commonly used in the industry to get to
           the underlying cause of problems or trigger events, to provide insight for the
           management of future risks helping to identify both operational and capital
           interventions that would eliminate, reduce or effectively mitigate risks. Further,

                   availability or cost; the more advanced and complex the RCA
                   methodology utilised should be…

                   intervention options should be incorporated into the water company

2.31.   Although this particular report was published outside of the relevant period for

        deﬁned root cause analysis process in response to incidents. We would expect

        analysis is not limited to identifying the trigger event as the cause of a supply

        identifying the underlying systemic issues, such as why and how the assets,
        their design, maintenance status/condition and operational response planning
        have contributed to such an interruption occurring and actions needed to

        eliminate a symptom of a problem, but not the problem itself.

2.74.   Providing reliable supplies of safe drinking water is a fundamental legal
        obligation of all water companies, reﬂected in their general duty under
        section 37 WIA91 to maintain a water supply system.


2.75.   As mentioned above, apart from GSS, no regulations setting out standards
        applicable to the section 37 WIA91 duty have been put in place to date. We have
        therefore applied the wording of this section, and other relevant provisions,
        based on its common-sense construction, to the facts of this case to assess
        South East Water's conduct and we did so in accordance with what we would
        expect from a reasonable company. We carefully and conscientiously considered
        the evidence available to us in this case and took into account the performance
        of other companies as well as industry practice.


2.76.   We explain our approach in further detail below, including a list of indicative
        behaviours/good practice which we consider a reasonable company must
        demonstrate in order to meet its duties under section 37 WIA91. This is a non-
        exhaustive list, which focuses on the aspects of supply systems relevant to this
        investigation.


2.77.   Water undertakers are required to develop and maintain an economical and
        efﬁcient water supply system. This means that its system must not only be
        delivered at proportionate cost but also be ﬁt for purpose: a system which, while
        low cost, cannot be sufﬁciently relied upon to meet the undertaker's supply
        obligations cannot be said to be economic and efﬁcient. Monitoring and
        maintenance of supply system assets, such that this system operates
        economically and efﬁciently, is a key aspect of this duty and applies to all
        components of a supply system such as boreholes, trunk mains and service
        reservoirs. We expect a reasonable water company to undertake not only
        reactive, but also proactive maintenance. We also expect the companies to have
        adequate operational response to issues with their supply systems, such as
        supply interruptions, to ensure that the system continues to operate
        economically and efﬁciently and minimise their impact on the customers.


2.78.   Whether something is economical or efﬁcient will ultimately be the matter of
        fact in the speciﬁc circumstances of each investigation, judged on the balance
        of evidence.


2.79.   We also expect the companies to have arrangements in place for providing water
        supplies and maintaining, improving and extending water mains and other pipes
        such that the company is both meeting its obligations in Part III WIA91 and that
        it is able to continue to do so (this involves determining whether a company is

2.80. We expect a reasonable company to take ownership of and be proactive in
            ensuring its compliance with section 37 WIA91. A reasonable company would
            invest to improve its water supply system in order to be able to comply with its
            duties and, where such investment is not possible, ensure that its existing
            assets are performing as well as they can through maintenance and operational
            response. Evidence as to whether or not a company appropriately sets and/or
            meets its maintenance and operational internal goals is relevant for the purpose
            of assessing a company's compliance with section 37 WIA91. We also consider
            the wider factual background such as developments with respect to climate
            change and Covid-19, to assess what a reasonable company ought to have
            known about regulatory expectations and risks to their water supply systems.


2.81.       In light of the above, we expect a reasonable company to, as a minimum, do the
            following in order to comply with its section 37 WIA91 duties:


        •     Maintain key assets through proactive planned preventative maintenance and
              regular inspection to ensure supply resilience, particularly those assets which
              are single points of failure. We would expect that a reasonable company would
              adequately assess the impact that a planned outage would have on demand,
              consider any existing assets that may be out of service, and maintain
              sufﬁcient operational resources to avoid or reduce the severity of any loss of
              supply. For high demand or critical periods (i.e. summer and winter) we would
              expect a 'hands off' process when planning for maintenance with a clear,
              robust and auditable escalation process to ensure that the cumulative, real-
              world risk, interdependencies and consequence of ongoing works is assessed
              and either mitigated or triggers a "do not work" instruction.
        •     For service reservoirs, a maximum ten-year inspection cycle and aim for a
              year-round normal operation volume target of 80-85% of the total volume of
              the service reservoir.
        •     Maintain supply demand balance and headroom at a level that would ensure a
              secure and reliable water supply to premises in all of its areas. A reasonable
              company would maximise storage and therefore resilience in periods of
              historically high demand or leakage. Prior to predicted extreme weather
              events, a reasonable company would increase storage in reservoirs and
              increase detection and repair activity to resolve leaks on the network.

3.2.3 South East Water's planning processes
3.49. This section provides an overview of South East Water's planning processes that
      it uses, amongst other things, to manage supply resilience risks and its water
        resource management more generally. We have reviewed its WRMPs, corporate
        risk register, Executive and Board reporting processes and its area plans for the

Water resource management planning process

3.50. The WIA91145 requires water companies to prepare and maintain a WRMP which
      sets out companies' intended approach to maintain a supply demand balance
        surplus for at least the next 25 years 146 and achieve a secure supply of water for
        customers and a protected and enhanced environment. 147 WRMPs should be
        prepared at least every ﬁve years, with annual reviews that include clear
        information regarding WAFU.148


3.51.   Part of the WRMP includes ensuring opportunities to supply other water
        companies or regional groups if a surplus of water exists. WRMPs should have no
        planning deﬁcits over the planning period and if there is a surplus, or there are
        additional sources available, companies should consider supply options with
        neighbouring companies or regional groups to see if this surplus is available for
        trading. 149 South East Water has stated that it is becoming less common to see a
        supply demand surplus for its area. 150


3.52.   Companies report on progress in delivering their WRMPs in annual reviews
        which they submit to Ofwat and the Environment Agency for review. Annual
        reviews include information on maintaining actual supply demand balance
        against the forecast provided in the WRMP, meeting forecasts for demand
        reductions (such as reducing leakage), and delivering supply schemes which
        contribute to the supply demand balance. Companies must also report on risks
        to delivery against WRMP forecasts, how these risks impact the ability to

3.53. As part of the WRMP, companies assess supply and demand forecasts.
        Companies' initial forecasts (Baseline Plan) include an assessment of WAFU,
        which represents the supply available in a speciﬁed design event (i.e. a drought
        with a 0.5% or 0.2% annual exceedance probability) from resources and
        transfers external to the WRZ. This is the supply available after outage and
        losses have been accounted for, as well as future factors to supply availability
        such as climate change and environmental abstraction reductions. WAFU
        typically declines over the planning horizon as a result of the future factors
        considered. Baseline demand forecasts include an assessment of demand from
        customers (household, that is, PCC, and non-household), plus losses such as
        leakage, in a specified design event. The baseline demand forecast also includes
        future factors affecting demand, such as population and industry growth, and
        therefore baseline demand forecasts typically rise over the planning horizon.


3.54.   The ﬁnal planning forecasts involved in the WRMP process (Final Plan) include
        an assessment of baseline WAFU and demand forecasts, plus new supply and
        demand side options proposed to be implemented over the planning horizon. As
        such, the Final Plan WAFU forecasts are typically higher than the Baseline Plan,
        and demand forecasts typically lower. We consider the Final Plan WAFU
        forecasts to be the most appropriate supply forecast against which to compare a
        company's actual demand. This compares how the company has planned to
        deliver sufﬁcient capacity and a resilience system with the actual demands
        experienced.


3.55. Companies also assess supply and demand forecasts based on different types of
      scenarios, including 'baseline dry year annual average' (DYAA) and 'baseline dry
        year critical period (peak week) demand' (DYCP). Companies set out in their
        Final Plan which scenario is critical to their plans, depending on any
        constrictions to their supply demand balances. We consider DYCP to be most
        aligned with company's planning for extreme events as opposed to the DYAA
        scenario which averages dry conditions across the year.

3.61.   To manage risks across its WRZs, South East Water has a Corporate Risk Register

3.71.       Asset health checks and maintenance are essential to maintaining resilient

            sufﬁcient to manage asset risks and maintain reliable services for customers.

Ofwat's ﬁndings on asset maintenance
3.156. Below we set out our ﬁndings relating to South East Water's monitoring and
       maintenance of its water supply system and its compliance with section 37
        WIA91 and Condition P12.

General approach to maintenance
3.157. As set out in Section 2 above, under section 37 WIA91, water undertakers are
       required to develop and maintain an economical and efﬁcient supply system,
        that is – a supply system that is ﬁt for purpose. A system delivered and
        maintained at a proportionate cost, but which cannot be relied on to meet an
        undertaker's supply, [water quality] and other obligations, is not economic and
        efﬁcient. Monitoring and maintenance of supply system assets, such that this
        system operates economically and efﬁciently, is a key aspect of this duty and
        applies to all components of a supply system such as boreholes, trunk mains and
        service reservoirs. Water undertakers are also required to have arrangements in
        place to provide water supplies and maintain, improve and extent water mains
        such that they are able to continue to meet their supply, [water quality] and
        other Part III WIA91 obligations, i.e. to ensure there is not a real risk they would
        not be able to comply with these obligations.


3.158. The evidence shows that throughout the Relevant Period; South East Water has
       not been as proactive in terms of maintaining its assets as a reasonable water
       company should have been. South East Water has not updated its Area Plans
       since 2019 and 2020, and we have seen no evidence that it has delivered on the
       mitigating actions it identiﬁed in the Area Plans. While the introduction of AIPOS
       may assist in prioritisation and risk management may assist in future, there is
       limited evidence of a proactive approach to maintenance prior to this. This is
        evident as from as from as early as its CRR Board reports in 2018 South East
        Water identiﬁed a "lack of proactive monitoring of asset availability" 358 this
        continued to be a feature of its Area Plans in 2019 and 2020 with "very little"
        ability to monitor performance of its sites, assets and network. This continued
        into January 2022 with staff raising concerns about lack of knowledge of the
        network and South East Water itself identifying the need for further root cause
        analysis to support its understanding of its network. We examine the importance
        of root cause analysis, including with respect to asset health and maintenance
        in Section 3.3.2.

      for the company would have been to focus on what actions might be undertaken

Summary of ﬁndings and conclusions on section 37 WIA91
3.199. We ﬁnd that South East Water has contravened its section 37 WIA91 duty, as it
         has not been maintaining an economic and efﬁcient system of supply within its
         Eastern region. By failing to adequately maintain its assets, it has failed to
         ensure that it has arrangements in place in its Eastern region, for providing
         supplies of water to meet demand and maintaining and improving its mains,
         such that it is able to continue to meet its domestic supply and [water quality]
         obligations. More speciﬁcally, South East Water has:
     •     Failed to ensure its service reservoirs were adequately and regularly
           inspected (at least every 10 years) and cleaned/maintained. This has led to
           degradation in condition of its reservoirs and an increase in the risks to water
           quality and loss of supply.
     •     Failed to maintain storage levels at service reservoirs during periods of high
           demand. We found that key service reservoirs entered critical periods with low
           storage levels.
     •     Failed to adequately maintain its trunk mains by undertaking sufﬁcient
           preventative maintenance and over-relying on reactive maintenance. Trunk
           mains have been identiﬁed as a factor that has at least contributed to supply
           interruptions in the Eastern region.
     •     Failed to undertake the necessary inspection and maintenance of boreholes,
           which led to boreholes becoming non-operational and increased the risk of
           outages at boreholes, contributing to supply interruptions. On several
           occasions, boreholes were out of service or underperforming during high
           demand periods while other assets were taken out of service, leading to
           reduced yield. We also found that South East Water has failed to optimise the
           yield of its non-operational boreholes to provide additional supply resilience
           and delayed re-prioritising its borehole maintenance programme.
     •     Failed to plan for maintenance of key assets outside of critical or high
           demand periods. We found a lack of holistic risk assessment to ensure
           sufﬁcient headroom and anticipate the impact of outages on demand to allow
           for planned preventive maintenance without the need to shut down
           operations. We would expect that a reasonable company would adequately
           assess the impact that the outage would have on demand, consider any

           to a revised leakage strategy, however, it is difﬁcult to map these actions
           against the root cause.
     •     Flooding at site: South East Water refers to a feasibility study for two water
           treatment works but it does not explain the reason for the ﬂooding or list the
           root cause(s) of the ﬂooding which may have led to the selected option to
           investigate ﬂood defences.
     •     Turbidity: South East Water mentions this is due to scouring. This does not
           address the 'why' question – it is unclear if the company has explored if there
           are any issues with the design of assets, underlying maintenance or operator
           related issues; or if there are any methodologies that need review for how this
           is undertaken; for example, ﬂushing regime, valve operations etc.

3.289. The above indicates that South East Water did not undertake meaningful root
       cause analysis during the Relevant Period, despite “identifying the root cause”
       being a stated component of its own six-stage methodology. Had such analysis
       been carried out, the company would have recognised internal factors as well as
       external and root causes rather than immediate causes or trigger events (such
       as high demand or extreme weather). For an investigation of the root cause of
       an event of this signiﬁcance, we would expect the documents to show
       consideration of broader organisational issues, such as, the need for
       improvements in business process control (e.g. training, incident management,
         operational control), which they did not. Further, South East Water's analysis
         moves directly to conclusions/recommendations (e.g. action plans, optioneering
         and capital programmes), without providing a summary of data/evidence it
         investigated and its analytical process, which make it difﬁcult to map the causal
         factors and proposed actions. This is further underscored by the fact that,
         during the minded-to process, South East Water sought clarification from us on
         the definition of root cause analysis. A reasonable company would ensure that it
         has a good understanding of this concept and develop internal processes to
         conduct effective root cause analysis. We conclude that South East Water does
         not understand how to do a thorough root cause analysis or have such internal
         processes in place.

       way to address issues identiﬁed in its root cause analysis (although further

3.310. Our ﬁndings demonstrate that while South East Water has failed to properly

       extreme weather events, including by failing to maintain sufﬁcient headroom;

         contravened section 37 WIA91 as it has failed to put appropriate planning
         processes in place in order to maintain its water supply system and meet its
         domestic supply obligation. Given the issues raised in our investigation, we

Lessons learnt from the Events
3.345. We have found that South East Water has failed to effectively implement the
       lessons from previous events. Despite over 70% of the actions in the 2018 Freeze
       Thaw Event Action Plan having future completion dates, South East Water did
       not provide details of monitoring or implementation plans to ensure that the
       actions it suggested would be implemented effectively and to mitigate the
       impact of similar events in the future. From the evidence provided, South East
       Water did not holistically review the actions from the 2018 Freeze Thaw Event
       until four years later, following the 2022 Freeze Thaw Event. South East Water's
       review of the 2022 Freeze Thaw Event was, once again, only following requests
       by Ofwat and the DWI that all water companies review their performance. This is
       a reactive approach.

3.346. Further, South East Water's review of the 2022 High Demand Event was
       published in August 2023, almost a year after the event and after the 2023 High
       Demand Event. Therefore, any actions regarding drought and incident
       management from 2022 were not actioned in time for the 2023 High Demand
       Event, which is again a failure of South East Water's systems of planning and
       ability to learn from past events. This delay in actioning lessons learnt from
       Events within the Relevant Period indicates a failure to take steps to ensure a
       strong operational response to incidents, regularly test the effectiveness of
       incident plans and to take steps to address any vulnerabilities identiﬁed.


3.347. This failure to learn lessons and review incident plans, was compounded by
       South East Water's failure to undertake sufﬁcient root cause analysis to identify
       the underlying cause of supply interruptions, which would have identiﬁed
       appropriate action (as detailed in Section 3.3.2). South East Water maintains
       that "a comprehensive analysis of the root causes of the supply system
       resilience issues we encountered during high demand events in AMP7 (2020–25)

4. Our ﬁndings
4.1.   As required by sections 20 and 22A(4) of the WIA91, in this section we set out the
       statutory provisions and relevant licence conditions that we consider South East
       Water has breached and explain our assessment of the evidence we have
       considered in reaching our conclusions. We have also already set out our more
       detailed ﬁndings with respect to speciﬁc areas of South East Water's activities
       and performance in relation to its water supply system in Section 3.3.


4.2.   In the following sections, we consider each of the statutory provisions and
       relevant licence conditions that we consider South East Water has breached.

Section 37 WIA91: failure to maintain a water supply
system
4.3.   Maintaining water supplies to customers is a fundamental duty of water
       companies and vital to meeting the conditions of section 37 WIA91 and other
       duties. We have found several failures by South East Water to maintain an
       efﬁcient and economical system of water supply that in of themselves and
       collectively constitute a breach of section 37 WIA91. We made ﬁndings in section
       3.3 about South East Water's maintenance of key assets, its inadequate planning
       and its poor operational response and preparedness to the Events within the
       Relevant Period. This demonstrates a failure to develop and maintain an efﬁcient
       and economical system of water supply within its Eastern region and, separately,
       to ensure all such arrangements have been made for providing water supply to
       meet demand, as is necessary for securing its obligations under Part III. We
       have also found that South East Water has failed to ensure all such
       arrangements have been made for the provision of water supply and demand
       and for maintaining, improving and extending water mains, with respect to
       trunk mains repair and replacement, as are necessary for securing South East
       Water's obligations under Part III. We consider these are individual breaches of
       section 37 WIA91 but also when taken together indicate a widespread failure to
       maintain an economic and efﬁcient supply system and make arrangements
       required to meet its Part III obligations, in this case, its domestic supply duty
       and duties related to water quality.


4.4.   We recognise that other companies may have failed in certain respects in the
       past and during the Events within the Relevant Period. However, South East
       Water is the company that is consistently underperforming regarding supply
       interruptions and its handling of extreme weather. The number of ﬁndings
       identiﬁed in Section 3.3 demonstrate real issues with maintenance, planning

           and operational response and how South East Water maintains its supply
           system. Without further action from the company, we consider there is a real
           risk of supply interruptions in the future and that the company will continue to
           not meet its domestic supply duty. These issues have a real impact on
           customers, particularly those customers at "pinch points" at the "end-of-the-
           line" who disproportionately experienced supply interruptions compared with
           South East Water's Western region and other companies in the south east of
           England.


4.5.       Based on the evidence and ﬁndings set out in Section 3, we are satisﬁed that,
           during the Relevant Period, South East Water has contravened and is continuing
           contravene its duty under section 37 WIA91 by failing to develop and maintain an
           efﬁcient and economical system of water supply within its Eastern region and,
           separately, to ensure all such arrangements have been made for providing water
           supply to meet demand, as is necessary for securing its obligations under Part
           III, speciﬁcally:
       •     Failings in the inspection and maintenance of service reservoirs – South East
             Water did not ensure that service reservoirs were inspected, cleaned, and
             maintained at appropriate intervals, including the expected maximum ten-
             year inspection cycle. As a result, asset condition deteriorated over time,
             increasing the risks to both water quality and continuity of supply.
       •     Failings in the management of storage levels in advance of and during
             critical periods– South East Water did not adequately manage storage to
             maintain sufficient headroom at service reservoirs. We identified instances
             where key reservoirs entered high-risk periods with critically low storage
             levels, heightening the likelihood and severity of supply interruptions.
       •     Failings in the inspection, maintenance, and optimisation of boreholes –
             Inadequate inspection and maintenance resulted in boreholes becoming non-
             operational or underperforming, increasing the risk of outages. On several
             occasions, boreholes were unavailable during periods of high demand while
             other assets were also out of service, reducing overall system yield. In
             addition, South East Water did not take timely steps to optimise the output of
             non-operational boreholes or to reprioritise its borehole maintenance
             programme to improve supply resilience.
       •     Failings in maintenance planning and risk assessment of key assets – South
             East Water did not adequately plan maintenance activities outside of critical or
             high demand periods and lacked a holistic assessment of system-wide risks.
             In particular, it did not sufficiently assess the cumulative impact of asset
             outages on available supply or ensure that adequate operational headroom
             and resources were in place to avoid or mitigate loss of supply events. Nor did
             it mitigate known risks posed by extreme weather and climate change,

Licence Condition P12: South East Water's systems of
planning and internal control
4.5       Licence Condition P12 requires a company to act in a manner best calculated to
          ensure that it has in place sufﬁcient ﬁnancial and management resources and
          systems of planning and internal control to carry out its regulated activities,
          both now and for the foreseeable future.


4.6       South East Water should have understood its legal and regulatory obligations,
          including those relating to section 37 WIA91 outlined above, and have put in
          place appropriate processes and controls to ensure that it was able to operate
          its water supply system assets in a manner that complied with those obligations.
          It should have in place systems to ensure that any non-compliance (and the risk
          of non-compliance) is escalated within the company and that prompt, timely
          investigations are carried out and remedial action taken to secure compliance.
          It should also have internal controls in place that follow-up these interventions
          to ensure that compliance is achieved in a timely and effective manner.


4.7       We found that South East Water was, at best, reactive with respect to
          maintenance, which is not the approach of a reasonable company planning to
          meet its regulated activities. The evidence outlined in Section 3 shows an
          overarching failure of South East Water to maintain its supply system at a
          sufﬁcient production capacity to meet periods of peak demands and that its
          asset base was operating at a level that did not support proper functioning of its
          water supply system. South East Water's Executive Team and Board were aware
          of these issues and should have been doing more to improve its compliance,
          including with respect to its operational response to Events in the Relevant
          Period, with its regulated activities in section 37 WIA91 and the SEMD.

5. Proposal to issue an enforcement order
Background
5.1.   Under section 18 WIA91, if we are satisﬁed that a regulated company is
       contravening or likely to contravene a condition of its Licence or a statutory
       requirement we are under the duty to make an enforcement order containing
       such provisions as are requisite to secure compliance with that condition or
       requirement.


5.2.   Under section 19 WIA91, we are not required to make an enforcement order if we
       are satisﬁed that the contravention in question is of a trivial nature, or is
       contrary to our duties in Part I WIA91, including our duty to have regard to best
       regulatory practice and our other duties under section 2 WIA91, explained in
       more detail in Section 2 above. We may also instead or in part accept formal
       undertakings from a company to take remedial steps as long as we consider
       them appropriate to secure compliance. A company's obligation to comply with
       an undertaking is treated as a statutory requirement which is enforceable by
       Ofwat under section 18 WIA91. As also explained above, in carrying out our
       enforcement duty under section 18 WIA91, we must also have regard to the
       desirability of promoting economic growth.


5.3.   In pursuance of the duties described above, and having regard to the growth
       duty guidance, we have therefore sought to ensure these proposed enforcement
       order measures are proportionate to the extent of non-compliance we have
       found and a company returns to compliance as quickly and efﬁciently as
       reasonably possible, consistent with what the company can reasonably deliver.


5.4.   Under section 22 WIA91, where a company fails to comply with an enforcement
       order, Ofwat may apply to the Court to seek an injunction to compel a company
       to do so or for other forms of appropriate relief. Section 22 WIA91 also makes
       clear that the obligation to comply with an enforcement order constitutes a duty
       owed to any person who may be affected by a contravention of the order. That
       person may bring legal proceedings against a company if a breach of that duty
       causes them to sustain loss or damage.


5.5.   Further information regarding considerations relevant to enforcement orders
       can be found in our published guidance (Enforcement Guidance here by
       hyperlink).

Relevant provisions of the WIA91
6.1.    Under section 22(1)(a) and 22A(2)(a) of the WIA91, Ofwat may impose on the
        water or sewerage company a penalty of such amount (not exceeding 10% of the
        regulated company's relevant turnover in a relevant year) as is reasonable in all
        the circumstances of the case, where it is satisﬁed that the company has
        contravened or is contravening any condition of its Licence, or any statutory
        requirement Ofwat is responsible for enforcing.


6.2.    Under section 22A(11) of the WIA91, no penalty imposed by Ofwat under section
        22A may exceed 10% of the turnover of the company, determined in accordance
        with the Water Industry (Determination of Turnover for Penalties) Order 2005.
        Article 3 of that Order provides for the purposes of section 22A(11) of the WIA91,
        the relevant turnover of a company is the applicable turnover for the preceding
        business year net of tax (that is, the last business year preceding the date on
        which Ofwat gives notice under section 22A(4) of the WIA91). Article 2(2) deﬁnes
        "applicable turnover" as "the amounts, determined in conformity with normal
        accounting practice in the United Kingdom, which are derived by a company
        from the provision of goods and services, in the course of the company's
        regulated activities in respect of which the penalty is imposed" and Article 2(1)
        deﬁnes "regulated activities" as: "(a) in the case of a company holding an
        appointment as a water undertaker, its functions as a water undertaker." In this
        case, the regulated activities in question are related to South East Water's
        activities as a water company. As South East Water is a water only company, this
        captures all of its activities, represented by its total appointed revenue.

        applicable turnover derived from its activities as a water company in that
        business year was £280.811 million. 605 Accordingly, the maximum penalty that
        we could impose on the company would be 10% of that number i.e.

6.10. As set out in Section 3 and Section 4, we are satisﬁed that South East Water has
      contravened section 37 WIA91 and Licence Condition P12 in relation to how it
            managed, operated and maintained its water supply system during the Relevant
            Period. We note that in this document we have considered the broader context
            for South East Water's conduct preceding the Relevant Period to understand
            whether the company should have been aware of the risks to its water supply
            system and/or learned lessons from the issues it had experienced, including its
            performance during the 2018 Freeze Thaw Event. However, we have not applied
            a penalty with respect to the company's conduct prior to the Relevant Period.


6.11.       In determining whether to impose penalties for these contraventions, we have
            had regard to Ofwat’s Statement of policy with respect to ﬁnancial penalties and
            in particular the following factors, as further detailed below:
        •     The seriousness and duration of the contraventions or failure.
        •     If the contravention or failure has damaged the interests of customers, the
              degree of harm caused, and any increased costs incurred by customers.
        •     If the application of a penalty would be likely to create an incentive to comply
              and deter future contraventions or failures.
        •     Any gains made by the company (financial or otherwise).
        •     Any damage to other market participants.
        •     Any damage caused to the environment.
        •     Whether the contraventions or failure was or is of a trivial nature.
        •     Whether the contravention or possibility of a contravention would have been
              apparent to a diligent company.
        •     Precedents set under equivalent provisions for other utilities.

6.12.       In considering these factors we rely on the evidence gathered in each speciﬁc
            case.

Seriousness and duration of the contravention

6.13.       As a general duty, section 37 WIA91 is one of the core obligations of a water
            company. Licence Condition P12 similarly relates to fundamental requirements
            for a company to act in the manner best calculated to be able to fulﬁl its
            functions and duties. We therefore consider a contravention of these provisions
            to be serious.

6.14.   The evidence of our ﬁndings in Sections 3 and 4 shows that South East Water
        has failed to maintain, manage and operate key assets within its asset base in
        the manner we would expect from a reasonable company, with respect to both
        section 37 WIA91 and Licence Condition P12, and that it is currently still
        contravening those provisions. As set out in detail in Sections 3 and 4, these
        failings are widespread across different asset types and concern the key aspects
        of running a water supply system, namely: failure to timely, effectively and
        proactively inspect and maintain a number of key assets, in line with the basic
        expectations we have of a reasonable company, failure to effectively plan for
        critical demand periods, and failures in operational response to address the
        underlying issues and assist the customers affected by the supply interruptions
        and emergencies. They have persisted over an extended period of time (at least
        ﬁve years going back to 2018) in all WRZs in the Eastern region, resulting in
        South East Water failing to deliver the continuity of supply expected by
        customers and putting water quality and future supply at a signiﬁcant risk. They
        stem from its failure to address known vulnerabilities in the Eastern region that
        were known to the company from at least the start of the Relevant Period.
        Throughout our ﬁndings, we have highlighted the impact on customers of these
        failures, including those repeatedly affected by Events during the Relevant
        Period particularly customers at the "end-of-the-line" (we discuss this further
        below). In addition, our ﬁndings in Sections 3 and 4 demonstrate that South
        East Water has not historically had an adequate understanding of how its assets
        have been operating in practice, and, to date, has failed to undertake basic
        adequate root cause analysis that we would expect of a reasonable company to
        get to the underlying cause of issues with its supply system. Instead, South East
        Water relies on its view that the root cause of Events during the Relevant Period
        was "extreme weather" or "high demand" (rather than these being triggering
        factors), and did not seek to ﬁnd out internal asset heath, process and planning
        related causes that led to repeat instances of non-compliance. As set out in
        Sections 3 and 4, these breaches are ongoing.

Conclusion on the appropriateness of ﬁnancial penalty and its broad level

6.31.   Having considered the factors above, we are satisﬁed that a ﬁnancial penalty is
        appropriate in this case. As discussed in Section 4 above, we have found that
        South East Water contravened its duties and obligations under section 37 WIA91
        and Licence Condition P12 and that these contraventions were serious in nature.
        The contraventions are interrelated to an extent and their combined effect
        impacts on the seriousness of South East Water's conduct as a whole. Therefore,
        we propose to impose a single penalty, rather than separate penalties in respect
        of each breach.

6.32. In setting the broad penalty level, we have taken the factors above into account,
        as well as both the cumulative effect of all breaches and the degree of overlap
        between them. We recognise that the scope of this investigation and the impact
        of South East Water's failings we identiﬁed in this document concern the
        Eastern region, not the entire area for which South East Water is the undertaker.
        We considered whether this should be reﬂected in the level of penalty we
        propose to impose on the company. The Eastern region covers the majority of
        the company's WRZs and, as discussed above and shown in our ﬁndings, the
        failings with respect to this region and the impact on customers (discussed
        further below) were widespread, longstanding and particularly serious. We have
        previously warned companies that penalties for future breaches would increase
        and that we would take action if the industry did not improve its operational

         justify setting the proposed broad level of penalty at a relatively high level of 8%
         of the company's relevant turnover.


6.33. We also consider that this broad penalty level is consistent with our approach in
      previous decisions dealing with compliance with core duties. As above,
         companies have been on notice since our case against Thames Water in 2018,
         which resulted in ﬁnancial commitments equivalent to a ﬁne of 3% of turnover
         of their duty to comply with section 37 WIA91. Ofwat made clear in its open letter
         to industry at the time it reached settlement decision with Southern Water
         equivalent to a ﬁne of 6.7% that going forward companies could expect ﬁnes to
         increase for serious breaches of principal duties.


6.34. We have since issued a ﬁne of 9% of turnover to Thames Water for serious
      breaches of section 94 WIA91, the wastewater equivalent to section 37 WIA91,
      and accepted undertakings and redress packages calibrated according to the
      severity of the breach. We consider that the proposed ﬁne is consistent with this
      practice given the severity and duration of the failures we have uncovered in
      SEW’s Eastern Region and wider governance.

6.35. As set out in our Statement of Policy, other aggravating and mitigating factors

     •     The continuation of a contravention or failure.
     •     Any involvement of senior management.
     •     Any attempts to conceal the contravention or failure.
