A.3.1   On 16 February 2018 the Met ofﬁce provided an early warning of the potential for
        very cold weather and snow for the UK. On 23 February 2018, the Met Ofﬁce
        issued its ﬁrst yellow warning for snow for 26 February 2018. South East Water's
        region experienced below zero or near zero temperatures from 26 February 2018
        to 3 March 2018. On 3 March 2018 there was an increase in temperature of more
        than 10 degrees resulting in a rapid thaw of the snow and frozen ground. This
        led to an increase in South East Water's mains burst rate, with 216 bursts
        reported and repaired during the freeze thaw event. 615 South East Water
        experiences an increase in demand by over 20%. South East Water calculated
        that 105Ml/d extra was required, 18Ml/d due to bursts on its network and the
        remaining 87Ml/d was due to customer pipes and taps.

cards.body:
May 2025




Notice of Ofwat’s decision to
issue an enforcement order
and impose a financial penalty
on Thames Water
        Notice of Ofwat’s decision to issue an enforcement order and impose a financial penalty
                                           on Thames Water


Contents

1.   Introduction                                                                            7

2. Relevant background                                                                       9

3. Our investigation                                                                        48

4. Our assessment and findings                                                             129

5. Our decision to issue an enforcement order                                              161

6. Our decision to impose a financial penalty                                              167

A1: Enforcement Order                                                                      181

A2: Summary of Responses to Consultation                                                  190

A3: List of potentially non-compliant sites by category                                    210

A4: List of sites covered by Compliance First plan                                         214

A5: List of high spilling storm overflows                                                  217

A6: List of sites at which Thames Water has conducted SOAF assessments                     223

A7: Penalties framework                                                                   233




                                                 1
        Notice of Ofwat’s decision to issue an enforcement order and impose a financial penalty
                                           on Thames Water


About this document

This document constitutes a notice under section 22A(6) of the Water Industry Act 1991. It
sets out our decision to impose a financial penalty on Thames Water as a result of its
contraventions of the Urban Waste Water Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations 1994,
section 94 of the Water Industry Act 1991 and Condition P of its Licence. It also includes an
enforcement order under section 18 WIA91 requiring Thames Water to remedy the
contraventions that we have identified.

This decision follows the publication, on 6 August 2024, of a consultation on our proposal to
impose an enforcement order and a financial penalty on Thames Water. This document
summarises the evidence that we have gathered and sets out our findings in relation to the
issues under investigation, including why we believe that Thames Water has contravened its
statutory duties and the obligations of its Licence. It summarises the responses we received
to the draft decision and how we have taken those into consideration in reaching our final
decision.




                                                 2
          Notice of Ofwat’s decision to issue an enforcement order and impose a financial penalty
                                             on Thames Water


Executive summary

This notice describes the findings of our investigation in relation to Thames Water’s failings
and how these have occurred. The failings relate to the management, operation,
maintenance and performance of its wastewater treatment works (WWTW) and the
collecting systems (that is, its sewer networks – the network) that are used to supply them.
These are vital assets that are used to clean and treat sewage (or wastewater 1) and which
have a direct impact on the environment, particularly bodies of water, such as rivers or
streams, into which wastewater is released.

It follows a lengthy investigation during which we made multiple detailed requests for
information and data to Thames Water. In addition, we have reviewed environmental
performance and spills data published by the Environment Agency and also considered
relevant information provided to Ofwat by stakeholders.

Having reviewed this information, we have identified that most of Thames Water's WWTW
have storm overflows associated with them that spill regularly to the environment. In 2021,
for example, over 70% of these storm overflows spilled on 20 or more occasions, with almost
30% spilling on more than 60 occasions. Thames Water has failed to demonstrate that these
spills resulted from exceptional circumstances, or that it would have been excessively costly
to address the spills from these storm overflows. Indeed, the information that we assessed
showed that at the majority of its highest spilling storm overflows, operational and asset
maintenance issues were identified as the reason for the high spills.

These high spill levels result from Thames Water not having built and appropriately operated
its WWTW, which is reflected in the number of its WWTW that failed to meet the operational
expectations of their environmental permit requirements in relation to flow to full treatment
(157 WWTW or almost two thirds of Thames Water's WWTW with FFT permits or Temporary
Deemed Consents); dry weather flow (ten WWTW) performance; or which were found to have
insufficient storm tank capacity. While the number of high spilling storm overflows on
Thames Water's network was much lower, it emerged that Thames Water had failed to
identify over 300 storm overflows on its network which had not been monitored, and in many
instances, were also unpermitted. We consider the problems identified to be systemic across
the company's asset base, and that they have been occurring since at least 2017.

The information we have gathered also showed us that Thames Water did not have
appropriate and robust processes and controls in place to ensure that it was able to properly
deliver its wastewater business in line with its legal obligations. It lacked adequate processes
to enable it to properly monitor and assess compliance with its legal and regulatory


1
    Wastewater and sewage may be used inter-changeably in this document.



                                                   3
        Notice of Ofwat’s decision to issue an enforcement order and impose a financial penalty
                                           on Thames Water

obligations and, even when it was aware of potential compliance risks across its WWTW
estate and on its network, it failed to take action to address those risks effectively and with
sufficient urgency. In addition, Thames Water's senior management and Board had
inadequate oversight in relation to the compliance of its assets.

We published a draft decision for consultation in August 2024, setting out these findings and
proposing to issue the company with an enforcement order and a financial penalty. (We had
previously provided Thames Water with a copy of our provisional findings in December 2023
and given it an opportunity to comment on these and to provide any additional evidence that
it considered relevant to our investigation). In response to our consultation, we received a
detailed response from Thames Water as well responses from a number of other
stakeholders. A summary of these responses is set out in Appendix A2.


Having reviewed the information obtained during the course of our investigation and having
considered the comments we received in response to the consultation on our draft decision,
we have now reached a final decision in this case.

We have concluded that Thames Water failed to meet the following duties and obligations:

   •   to ensure its WWTW perform sufficiently in terms of design, construction, operation
       and maintenance so that spills only occur in exceptional or unforeseeable cases
       (accounting for seasonal variations), subject to best technical knowledge available not
       entailing excessive cost (BTKNEEC), under Regulation 4(4) of the Urban Waste Water
       Treatment (England and Wales) Regulations 1994 (UWWTR);


   •   to ensure its collecting systems (network) are constructed, operated and maintained
       according to BTKNEEC, under Regulation 4(2) and Schedule 2 UWWTR;

   •   to provide effectual drainage of its local areas and to effectually deal with the contents
       of its sewers, under section 94 of the Water Industry Act 1991 (WIA91); and


   •   to ensure as a company that it is run efficiently and effectively in compliance with its
       statutory duties, under Condition P of its instrument of appointment (Licence).


Based on the evidence provided to us, these failures to comply were caused by the company:

   •   failing to operate and maintain its assets adequately, and to upgrade them where
       necessary, to ensure they provided sufficient performance in accordance with
       BTKNEEC.

   •   failing to put in place adequate processes, resources and systems to enable it to
       routinely monitor and maintain operational capacity and performance and hence to



                                                 4
        Notice of Ofwat’s decision to issue an enforcement order and impose a financial penalty
                                           on Thames Water

       ensure sufficient performance in accordance with BTKNEEC at its WWTW and to ensure
       that its sewer networks comply with the requirements of Schedule 2 UWWTR.

   •   failing to put in place adequate processes to identify and address emerging and
       present compliance risks and failures effectively and in a timely manner and
       responding to changes over time in the catchments served by its WWTW and network.

   •   failing put in place adequate processes and systems to ensure that its data gathering,
       verification and analysis processes were fit-for-purpose to make a reasonable
       assessment of compliance and respond to variances in data quality across its asset
       base.

   •   failing to ensure its Executive and Board received and/or sought sufficient information
       and assurance on the operational performance of the company's wastewater assets
       and their compliance with relevant legal obligations. This lack of adequate oversight
       resulted in the company's management failing to be aware of and/or failing to address
       compliance failures and risks.


Thames Water’s failure to operate and manage its WWTW and network appropriately has
meant that it has not minimised the adverse effects its disposal of wastewater can have on
the environment. This failure has resulted in unpermitted and premature spills of wastewater
from its WWTW and network - where wastewater has not gone through all of the treatment
processes it is supposed to before being released into the environment. Such spills impact on
the environment and can cause harm to the health and biodiversity of water bodies, the
ability of customers to use water bodies recreationally in a safe way, and on customer and
public trust in Thames Water, the wider water sector and its regulatory regime.

Thames Water has developed plans to restore compliance at 157 of its WWTW that it has
identified as potentially non-compliant with FFT and other environmental permit conditions
(what Thames Water terms its 'sites of concern'). These plans are expected to be delivered by
the end of AMP8, that is, by 2030. The company has also accelerated the roll-out of new
monitors and has implemented new tools to enable it to have a more timely view of what is
happening at individual sites. It has introduced new operational and governance
arrangements to ensure greater oversight of what is happening across its WWTW estate and
network; has made improvements to the way in which it identifies and manages risks; and
has taken steps to ensure a clearer line of sight for its Executive and Board in relation to the
performance of its wastewater assets and the company's compliance with its environmental
obligations.

Notwithstanding the measures that Thames Water has already introduced, or is proposing to
introduce, Ofwat considers that there are additional steps that the company needs to take in
order to ensure it is compliant with its legal and regulatory obligations. We also consider that
the contraventions that have taken place are sufficiently serious to warrant the imposition of
a significant penalty in this case. Ofwat has decided, therefore, to:



                                                 5
          Notice of Ofwat’s decision to issue an enforcement order and impose a financial penalty
                                             on Thames Water

     •     Issue an enforcement order under section 18 WIA91, requiring Thames Water to take
           particular steps to facilitate its compliance with UWWTR, Section 94 and Licence
           Condition P.
     •     Impose a financial penalty under section 22A WIA91 equivalent to 9.0% (£104.5
           million) of the company's relevant turnover from its wastewater business.

In reaching this decision we have taken account of Thames Water's financial position and
wider operational challenges in the context of our section 2 WIA91 duties. We do not consider

2.        Relevant background

2.1       This section provides background information on the provision, operation and
          maintenance of typical WWTW and sewerage systems; the relevant legislative
          framework for our investigation; and our approach to enforcement of the relevant
          provisions.

2.2       The provision, operation and maintenance of WWTW and sewerage systems is subject
          to a range of legal obligations which are linked to the overarching requirements of
          Regulation 4 UWWTR. These include requirements from the environmental permitting
          regime which are aimed at ensuring that assets operate within the parameters of the
          UWWTR and do not have an unacceptable impact on the environment. In England, the
          Environment Agency is responsible for setting, checking, and enforcing compliance
          with permits and has powers to take enforcement or other regulatory action with
          respect to permit compliance. The permit sets out aspects of how the asset should
          operate and conditions around discharges. The requirements are specific to the asset
          being permitted as the nature of the receiving water bodies will vary from place to
          place, as will the volume and characteristics of the wastewater the asset is dealing
          with.


Sewerage Systems

2.3       Sewerage systems collect foul sewage from bathroom and kitchens in homes and
          offices and wastewater from industrial processes. Sewerage systems have developed
          over many years and can also collect rainwater from varying sources such as roofs and
          roads. Therefore, the flows of wastewater in sewerage systems vary substantially
          between different systems, throughout the day, and with changes in weather.

2.4       There are two broad types of sewerage systems:

      •     A fully separate sewer system has two sets of pipes for foul sewage and rainwater
            with no interconnections. Some rainfall will infiltrate into the foul sewer system,
            however, from groundwater or via manhole covers.
      •     A combined sewer system has a single set of pipes that collect both foul sewage and
            rain from roofs, patios and driveways, etc.

2.5       The catchments of WWTW are made of one, or both, of these types of systems. Older
          urban catchments typically consist of a central combined sewer system that has been
          expanded by the connection of separate sewer systems over time. In England and
          Wales most of the sewer systems operate as combined sewer systems.

2.6       Sewerage systems transport flows of sewage and wastewater to a WWTW for treatment
          before it is discharged to the environment. Sewerage systems may have storm

                                                    9

                                           on Thames Water

       overflows, which enable the discharge of untreated sewage directly into a watercourse
       before it reaches the WWTW during unusually heavy rainfall. This prevents the WWTW
       from receiving more sewage than it can cope with and being overwhelmed and/or the
       sewage flowing back into people's homes. The sewage is a mixture of foul sewage and
       rainwater and is often termed storm sewage.

2.7    Storm overflows in the sewerage system are, in essence, a weir in the sewer pipe. The
       level of this weir should be far above that of the level of flow in the sewer that is due to
       foul sewage only, that is when it is not raining (termed dry weather flow - DWF). In a
       storm, flows in the sewer will increase as rainwater drains into it. If the rainfall is
       unusually heavy the flow will increase to above the level of the weir and the excess
       storm sewage will be discharged to the watercourse. Storm overflows are typically
       designed and operated to 'pass-forward' a set level of flow before such discharges
       begin. The pass-forward flow (PFF) has historically been expressed as a multiple of the
       flow level during dry weather. This is, in effect, a measure of how much the foul
       sewage has been diluted by rainwater. Where storm overflows have an environmental
       permit (permit), discharges from those storm overflows must comply with
       requirements set out in that permit. As explained below (see paragraph 2.15), these
       permits are issued by the Environment Agency, and set a series of conditions intended
       to protect the environment from harm from discharges. The PFF for that storm
       overflow is typically a condition in its permit.

2.8    Historically, a storm overflow may have been designed and permitted to discharge
       when the PFF exceeded six times the DWF. However, this was only a 'rule of thumb' to
       prompt consideration of whether the potential for environmental harm necessitated
       further action. This historical rule of thumb was replaced in the 1970s by an
       alternative calculation, often referred to as Formula A (set out below). Formula A is
       used today as a basis for setting minimum PFF rates at many storm overflows, often in
       conjunction with a simple estimation of the dilution rate of the storm sewage in the
       watercourse. The formula can be adjusted to suit local conditions, for example if a
       proportion of the catchment is a separate sewer system. More complex procedures,
       such as that set out in the Urban Pollution Management Manual, are also used to
       assess the potential for ecological harm using mathematical simulation of models of
       the river water quality and of the sewerage system.4

2.9    Storm overflows in the sewer network can operate inappropriately, causing
       environmental harm. This can result from:

       •     Population growth, which can result in increases in flow, potentially beyond the DWF
             level set in the permit.
       •     Urban creep, a term that refers to the increase in impermeable areas as, for
             example, gardens are paved over, which can result in more rainfall draining to
             sewers.

2.10       If a sewer's design is not increased to reflect this higher flow level, over time both of
           the above factors can contribute to an increase in the frequency and volume of
           discharges from storm overflows.

2.11       In addition, storm overflows can operate inappropriately due to inadequate
           maintenance, with the result that they are not operating to their designed capacity.
           For example, deposits of silt or fats and oils can build up in sewers. These deposits can
           restrict the ability of the system to pass forward sufficient flow. This can result in
           discharges from the storm overflow outside of unusually heavy rain. In severe cases,
           discharges can occur even when it is not or has not recently been raining. Such 'dry-
           day' discharges 5 of foul sewage can be highly polluting as the flow is not diluted by
           heavy rain.

2.12       If the operation of the storm overflow is unsatisfactory then improvements can be
           made to either reduce the frequency of discharges or to reduce the pollutants in the
           discharge. One way in which the frequency of discharges can be reduced is by
           providing a tank that stores the excess flow so it can be passed forward for treatment
           when the storm has passed. Where a permit requires that such storage is provided,
           the minimum volume of the storage tank is set out in the environmental permit. 6

2.13       Sewerage systems, in general, operate via gravity. Where this is not feasible, sewage
           pumping stations (SPS) are used to forward flows and the flows are pumped under
           pressure through rising mains. SPS in combined systems can also have storm
           overflows. There are many similarities in the operation of storm overflows at SPS and
           on the sewerage network. However, the satisfactory functioning of SPS storm

Wastewater treatment works

2.15   Discharges from WWTW must comply with requirements set out in legislation and
       environmental permits. An Environment Agency permit sets out aspects of how the
       works should operate. Among other things, it sets out the volume of flow that can be
       discharged following treatment on a dry day; the maximum concentration of specified
       pollutants in such discharges; and the peak flow capacity of the works. The permit
       conditions are specific to each WWTW as the nature of the receiving water bodies will
       vary from place to place, as will the volume and characteristics of the flows received
       by the works.

2.16   WWTW which serve smaller populations (typically a population equivalent (PE) 7 lower
       than 250) generally have descriptive permits which set out, in qualitative terms, how
       the WWTW should be maintained and operated. WWTW serving five or fewer properties
       may be operated under 'General Binding Rules' regulations.8

2.17   WWTW, except those serving very small populations, continually receive wastewater,
       and thus discharge treated effluent (the final effluent or FE). The permit sets a limit on
       the volume of fully treated effluent that can be discharged when flows are not
       influenced by rainfall and/or snowmelt, termed the DWF. This permitted flow volume,
       together with permit conditions around the quality of the final effluent, seeks to set an
       appropriate pollutant load that can be discharged to the receiving water without
       causing environmental harm.

2.18   A minority of WWTW do not have a DWF permit condition but instead a condition that
       sets a maximum discharge of wastewater per day. In regulating WWTW using a DWF

2.19   The DWF level takes account of the population within the catchment, the number and
       type of businesses that are also generating wastewater and the volume of water
       infiltrating into the sewer systems from the groundwater table.

2.20   DWF can be determined in two different ways 9 depending on whether it is for an
       existing WWTW with a flow meter, or is being estimated, for example in order to
       determine the impact of future population growth or when designing a new WWTW. In
       the latter case, DWF can be estimated using the equation DWF = PG + I + E, as used in
       determining storm overflow settings with Formula A (set out at paragraph 2.8 above).

2.21   Where flow metering data is available, DWF can be estimated from a statistical
       analysis of daily flow readings over a year. Research concluded that DWF can be
       estimated as the non-parametric 20-percentile value of a time series of measured
       total daily volumes (TDV). This is known as Q80. Q80 is calculated by taking the TDV
       for each day of the year and placing these flow numbers in ascending order. Q80 is the
       flow on the day that is lower than 80% of total flows recorded, that is, the 20-
       percentile (or seventy-third day), and is intended to reflect the average dry day. Using
       statistical approaches introduces some uncertainty so another measure, Q90, is used
       by the Environment Agency to assess compliance with DWF permit conditions. A site
       will breach its permit where it fails to achieve its Q90 three or more times in a five-
       year period 10. Q90 is calculated in the same manner as Q80 and represents the flow on
       the day that is lower than 90% of total flows recorded. The measured Q90 will always
       be lower than the measured Q80, and it provides greater allowance for year-on-year
       variability in the flow rates. Research has shown that if Q90 is above the DWF permit
       discharge limit, then one can have 95% confidence that the WWTW is operating above
       the DWF permit limit.

       sewerage system assets and their associated permit conditions must be maintained
       and kept under review to reflect any changes in the catchment they serve. Companies
       should plan ahead and identify where the risk of change may necessitate additional
       treatment or capacity. For example, when population growth due to new housing
       occurs a WWTW's capacity for DWF and its associated permit conditions on DWF may
       need to increase. The final effluent water quality permit conditions may
       correspondingly need to become more stringent to ensure the pollutant load

2.23   Infiltration of groundwater into sewers can be a significant part of DWF. The infiltration
       occurs when the groundwater table is higher than any gaps in the pipe joints and
       manhole chambers in the sewerage system. Infiltration can also occur where sewer
       pipes are fractured and have not been repaired. As the groundwater table varies with
       the weather, infiltration rates vary accordingly. Sewerage systems should be designed
       to cope with such variations that occur under normal local climatic conditions, 11 and
       maintained to ensure infiltration is as low as practicable.

2.24   As set out in the previous section, flow in a sewerage system, and thus the amount of
       flow a WWTW receives, can vary substantially over time. On a dry day, flow at a WWTW
       typically has two peaks, one in the morning as people get up and use the bathroom,
       and then again in the evening as people cook and put on their dishwashers, etc.
       WWTW must be able to cope with these peaks, and varying amounts of rainfall.

2.25   Permits thus can have a condition to ensure that the peak flows of foul sewage are
       always fully treated.12 This is the Flow to Full Treatment (FFT) requirement. This is
       distinct from the DWF in that it aims to ensure that there is sufficient treatment
       capacity to deal with peak flows coming to the works as opposed to stipulating the
       total volume of flow that can be discharged in a day.

2.26   WWTW serving fully separate sewerage systems may not have any assets dedicated to
       the treatment of storm sewage. This is because fully separate systems are expected to
       have only a minor response to rainfall. These WWTW fully treat all flows they receive.

2.27   The physical configuration of WWTW can differ from site to site. Storm sewage arriving
       at a WWTW is typically managed in the three broad configurations set out below.
       However, other systems such as land treatment are also used.

         1. WWTW with a storm overflow at the inlet only.

         2. WWTW with a Settled Storm Overflow (SSO) after storm tanks,
         3. WWTW with both a storm overflow at the inlet and an SSO.

2.28   All WWTW can have emergency overflows, for the same reasons as set out previously
       for SPS.

2.29   Storm overflows at the inlet of WWTW operate, in essence, the same way as storm
       overflows on the sewerage network. Storm overflows at the inlet of WWTW are typically
       designed with a PFF set at six times DWF or Formula A. The discharged storm sewage
       has no further treatment, other than screening to remove coarse solids. At WWTW with
       an inlet storm overflow only, all flows up to six times DWF/Formula A are fully treated.
       The full peak capacity of the WWTW will, thus, only be utilised in heavy rain.

2.30   WWTW with storm tanks operate differently. The main purpose of storm tanks is to
       store storm sewage and return it for treatment after the rainfall has subsided. Thus,
       the treatment process does not receive very dilute flows and the peak capacity (FFT
       level) can be set at lower than six times DWF.

2.31   At WWTW with storm tanks, when it is raining, and flows to the WWTW are in excess of
       the permitted FFT level, works operators have the option within the WWTW permits to
       divert flow to the storm tanks. The diversion of flows can continue until the sewers
       have drained down to the extent that flows are lower than the FFT level. At this point
       the storm sewage in the tanks will be transferred back to the works for treatment.
       Provided the volume of diverted flow does not exceed the capacity of the storm tanks
       no discharge to the environment will occur. If the storm is intense or sustained,
       generating more storm sewage than the tanks can cope with, the permit allows the
       operator to discharge to the environment.

2.32   The point at which flows are diverted to storm tanks from the main treatment process
       is normally after screening and the removal of grit (often termed preliminary
       treatment). Further settlement of pollutants can occur in the storm tanks, and
       therefore discharges via this route may be considered partially treated. However,
       during extremely heavy storms any settled pollutants may be flushed into the river.
       These overflows are often termed settled storm overflows to differentiate them from
       other types of storm overflows. As noted above, it is also possible that storm overflows
       located in the network are provided with storm tanks.

2.33   Operators must provide storm tanks of sufficient storage capacity to protect the
       environment and minimum volumes are typically specified in environmental permits.
       All other things being equal, a WWTW with a lower storm tank volume will have a
       higher frequency of settled storm overflow spills, and thus potentially environmental
       harm.

2.34   Current Environment Agency guidance states that storm tanks "must settle out solids
       and have a minimum capacity of 68 litres per head served or a storage equivalent of

       compliance. This should likely include using flow metering and other monitors unless
       compliance can be robustly assured by other means.

2.45   WWTW with a DWF greater than 50 m3 per day, and numeric quality limited, typically
       have a condition within their permits requiring final effluent flow to be monitored at
       least every 15-minutes to MCERTS Standard. 17 These meters are situated, typically but
       not always, at the point of the final effluent discharge, and record the total daily flow.
       This daily flow data, for a calendar year, is analysed to determine the Q80 and Q90 flow
       values used for establishing DWF levels. The data is reported annually to the
       Environment Agency as part of its process to monitor compliance with DWF permit
       requirements.

2.46   The Environment Agency required water companies to install Event Duration Monitors
       (EDM) on all storm overflows by December 2023. 18 The EDM records when a discharge
       to the environment starts and ends, but not the flow rate or volume. It does this,
       typically, by monitoring the flow level at the overflow weir. The number of spills and
       the total duration for which spills occur in the year, for each storm overflow, is
       reported annually to the Environment Agency and made publicly available.19 The
       number of spills is calculated according to the '12/24 spill count' method. This method
       counts multiple smaller spills that occur in quick succession as a single spill event, but
       longer duration spills as multiple spills. This ensures that the data properly reflects the
       significance of longer-duration spills, while recognising that multiple small events in
       close proximity may relate to waves of flow arriving at the works as rainfall travels over
       a catchment area.

2.47   As set out previously, WWTW have the option to spill to storm tanks when the
       permitted FFT level is reached or exceeded. To best establish therefore that a spill is
       permitted under the conditions of its permit, requires a flow monitor downstream of
       the point at which flows might spill (that is, to measure the flow going to treatment)
       and an EDM to record when a spill to the storm tank, or the environment for an inlet
       storm overflow, is occurring. With this instrumentation in place, for all the times a spill
       is indicated on the EDM, the flow meter must be reading a value equal to, or greater
       than, the FFT requirement.

2.48   Whilst the FFT requirement in permits is not new, the Environment Agency has more
       recently been working with water companies to further develop the permit conditions
       for FFT to provide additional assurance around the monitoring of FFT compliance (that
       is, the reporting requirements under the permit, rather than the requirement itself to
       meet FFT levels). For the purpose of monitoring compliance, the conditions stipulate
       that permit compliance can be considered to be achieved when 95% of the individual
       flow values exceed 92% of the overflow setting (that is, the FFT limit) when the works
       is discharging to the storm tanks, or to the environment if there are no storm tanks.
       This proxy is used for monitoring purposes in recognition of there being some margin
       of error (here, +/- 8%) in the accuracy of meter readings. Nevertheless, companies are
       expected to meet their FFT permit conditions all of the time.

Monitoring of storm overflows

2.53   Water companies are expected to classify their storm overflows.20 There are three
       classifications; satisfactory, substandard and unsatisfactory. In summary, an
       unsatisfactory storm overflow is one that spills when it has not been raining, causes or
       significantly contributes to environmental harm or operates in breach of permit. A
       substandard storm overflow is one that has a satisfactory environmental impact but
       does not meet current engineering standards, for example with respect to screening
       requirements.

2.54   The Environment Agency can review permits or take enforcement action when a storm
       overflow becomes unsatisfactory. Where necessary, an improvement condition can be
       set to ensure appropriate standards are met. These storm overflows should be
       addressed as soon as practicable, normally within three years. The Environment
       Agency applies water quality design standards when it issues permits for all new,
       improved or altered storm overflows, that depend on the potential environmental
       impact of the discharge.

2.55   Companies are also required to address substandard storm overflows over the medium
       to long term through their routine maintenance and renewal activities. Companies are
       expected to proactively undertake activities that prevent a storm overflow becoming
       unsatisfactory.

2.56   A storm overflow can become unsatisfactory when new legal requirements come into
       effect which it does not meet. In these instances, companies, in collaboration with the
       Environment Agency, should develop a solution for inclusion in the WINEP. Ofwat
       allows water companies funding to deliver these solutions within the price review
       process.

2.57   The Environment Agency and water companies developed the Storm Overflow
       Assessment Framework (SOAF), 21 which was finalised in June 2018, to prioritise the
       investigation and remediation of those storm overflows spilling the most and
       contributing the most harm. It formed the basis for identifying storm overflow work
       programmes for inclusion in PR19 business plans – with investigations included within
       WINEP for PR19, and resulting remediation solutions intended to be included in either
       PR19 or PR24. The SOAF states that it is intended "to address the problems caused by
       discharges from storm overflows considered to operate at too high a frequency. The
       framework will ensure that the water industry is proactively monitoring and managing
       the performance of its overflows in light of the pressures of growth, urban creep and

2.58   The SOAF sets out processes for investigation and remediation. It consists of five
       stages.

       Stage 1 - Identifies storm overflows that have exceeded spill frequency triggers 23 and
       assesses whether this is due to exceptional rainfall; due to maintenance issues; or due
       to insufficient hydraulic capacity. More specifically:
            • Exceptional rainfall – this does not refer to individual rainfall events, but
                rather the rainfall across the reporting year.
            • Asset maintenance 24 – this applies where the storm overflows and potentially
                parts of the upstream and downstream sewer network have not operated as
                designed/expected. Those storm overflows for which maintenance issues are
                identified as the cause of the high spill frequence are removed from the next
                stages of the SOAF assessment as these issues should instead be resolved
                through operational maintenance.
            • Hydraulic capacity - if the reason for a high spilling storm overflow is neither
                exceptional rainfall, nor asset maintenance, then it is classified under this
                category. This indicates there may be insufficient capacity (conveyance or
                storage) to cope with the sewage flow plus typical rainfall entering the
                network.

       Stage 2 - For the storm overflows where hydraulic incapacity is identified as the
       cause, the environmental impact of the discharges is quantified. This consists of two
       stages. Firstly, there is an aesthetic assessment, which considers amenity value,
       customer complaints and historical pollution incidents. Secondly an assessment of
       ecology is undertaken using invertebrate sampling. Where invertebrate sampling is
       not possible water quality is assessed through mathematical modelling.

       Stage 3 - The costs and benefits of improvement options for the storm overflow are
       determined. This identifies the environmental, social and economic benefits of
       overflow improvement to determine the most economically efficient improvement
       option.

General duty under section 94 WIA91

2.74      Under section 94(1) WIA91, wastewater companies have a general duty to:

        (a) provide, improve, and extend such a system of public sewers (whether inside their

            (whether inside their area or elsewhere) as is necessary from time to time for
            effectually dealing, by means of sewerage disposal works or otherwise, with the
            contents of those sewers.

2.75      As further detailed below, the duty imposed on every wastewater company by section
          94 WIA91 is supplemented by the UWWTR, which obliges companies to meet certain

          94. 29

Duties under Regulation 4 UWWTR

2.76      The permit regime described in paragraphs 2.15 to 2.61 above is aimed at ensuring

          industrial discharges. Regulation 4 UWWTR sets out specific requirements for the
          provision, maintenance and operation of WWTW and the sewerage systems which feed

2.83   The ECJ explained that to meet the objective of protecting the environment the
       concept of ‘sufficient performance’ referred to in Regulation 4(4) UWWTR (which
       applies to WWTW) must be understood to mean that under usual climatic conditions,
       and accounting for seasonal variations, all urban wastewater must be collected and
       treated. It clarified that non-compliance with the requirements of Regulation 4(4) in
       respect of the WWTW and Regulation 4(2) in respect of collecting systems could only
       be tolerated in exceptional or unforeseeable circumstances, such as 'unusually heavy
       rainfall'. The term 'unusual' is of key importance and means, again, that failure to
       collect or treat wastewater should not occur in normal circumstances.

2.84   The ECJ noted that the UWWTR do not prescribe a numerical spill threshold that would
       amount to a contravention. Accordingly, any discharge of untreated urban wastewater
       into the environment has the potential to constitute a breach of Regulation 4 UWWTR.
       From a practical perspective, Advocate General Mengozzi 36 noted in his Opinion on the
       case that the Commission had “on several occasions […] both during the pre-litigation
       phase and before the Court” indicated that “as a rule, exceeding the limit of 20
       overflows a year would be a cause for concern, suggesting a possible failure to fulfil
       obligations”. 37 While reiterating that “the Court cannot lay down numerical values
       which the legislature considered it appropriate to avoid”,38 he nevertheless expressed
       the opinion that “it may be entirely reasonable for the Commission to draw up
       quantitative guidelines on which to base its own monitoring activity”, 39 and that
       “[d]espite all its limitations and without prejudice to the need for a case-by-case
       assessment, a numerical criterion of that nature may be reasonable and
       acceptable.” 40

2.85   Within the UWWTR, the concept of BTKNEEC is only referred to expressly in relation to
       collecting systems (Regulation 4(2) UWWTR and paragraph 2 of Schedule 2 UWWTR).
       The ECJ clarified that BTKNEEC is also inherent in all of the UWWTR provisions which
       intend to secure the objective of protecting the environment. It therefore extends to
       WWTW in the context of controlling adverse environmental impacts arising from any
       discharges of untreated wastewater. BTKNEEC should be seen as a concept that
       enables compliance with the duties under the UWWTR without imposing unachievable
       obligations that could only be fulfilled at a disproportionate cost.

       very difficult to collect and treat all the waste water, it will be for the Member State

Practical implications of the legal framework for water
companies' operations and our approach to our investigation

2.93   The subsection below sets out some of the practical implications of the legal
       obligations set out above and what might reasonably be expected of a company to
       ensure that it is in compliance. It explains the approach we have taken to assessing
       the conduct under investigation. For the avoidance of doubt, the below is not an
       exhaustive discussion of all issues relevant to water companies' duties.

2.94   There is a considerable overlap between the requirements of Regulation 4(2) and 4(4)
       UWWTR, section 94 WIA91 and Licence Condition P12. We have therefore sought to
       indicate how each of the provisions may be relevant to the issues we discuss from our
       investigation.

2.95   What follows are practical implications of the various legal requirements and the
       approach that companies should be taking to compliance. These are relevant for our
       investigation's findings. How we have assessed Thames Water's conduct for the
       purpose of considering penalties in relation to breaches of these obligations is
       explained separately in Section 6.

Compliance with Regulation 4 UWWTR

2.96   Regulation 4(2) and 4(4) UWWTR require companies to "ensure" that their collecting
       systems and WWTW are providing sufficient performance, subject to the BTKNEEC test,
       which cannot be assumed or asserted but must be evidenced. This means that a
       company should not have any assets which do not meet this standard, and also that it
       should take active steps where appropriate to satisfy itself that its assets are
       compliant.

2.97   Ensuring that its assets are compliant means that a company should take ownership of
       monitoring its obligations under Regulation 4 UWWTR and adopt an inquisitive stance
       with respect to the performance of its assets. Where it becomes aware of indicators
       that an asset may not be performing sufficiently, for instance because spill data
       suggests that the asset is spilling outside of exceptional circumstances, Regulation 4
       requires the company to actively consider and investigate potential issues and not
       simply assume that the asset is compliant until proven otherwise. If there is spilling
       outside of exceptional circumstances, the ECJ has made clear that a BTKNEEC
       exception cannot be relied upon unless it has been made out in the specific case.

2.98   In our investigation we have considered both the extent to which the company's
       assets comply with the requirements of Regulation 4 UWWTR (that is, in terms of
       whether they are providing sufficient performance), and the extent to which the
       company has met its obligation under Regulation 4 to ensure that its assets continue

       to meet the relevant standards (that is, how it has gone about ensuring that they
       provide sufficient performance).




Spill prevention and mitigation

2.99   A company must ensure that wastewater flows to the environment (either directly or
       via storm tanks) which have not been fully treated only occur in exceptional or
       unforeseeable circumstances. Where it appears to a company that an asset may be
       spilling outside of exceptional circumstances, for instance because of the frequency of
       spills, the company should investigate the circumstances of the spill(s). If the
       discharges cannot be explained by exceptional circumstances (of whatever nature),
       the company must then mitigate any harm to the environment resulting from them to
       the extent that there is a remedy available which meets the BTKNEEC test. That
       remedy may be a change to operational processes or maintenance repairs (we note
       that under the SOAF, companies are required to resolve any operational or
       maintenance issues identified at Stage 1), or it could require physical works to change
       the capacity of the asset.

2.100 Non-compliance with these requirements might amount to a breach of Regulation 4(2)
      or 4(4) UWWTR (depending on whether the source of the discharge was the network or
      a WWTW), and consequently of section 94 WIA91. This non-compliance with Regulation
      4 is also interrelated with the general duty under section 94 WIA91 to provide and
      effectually deal with the contents of sewers and obligations as to the adequacy of a
      company's resources and systems of planning and internal control, and may be the
      result of shortcomings in these processes. A company in breach of Regulation 4
      UWWTR might therefore also be in breach of the broader duties under section 94
      WIA91 and Condition P. When assessing its compliance, a company should consider a
      number of factors, in particular the ones we identify below. These have been key
      considerations in our investigation.

2.101 The starting point to our assessment of compliance with Regulation 4 UWWTR is that
      all urban wastewater must be collected and treated under usual circumstances (in
      particular, in usual local climatic conditions). The circumstances in which spills might
      be tolerated at the first stage of the analysis are only truly unforeseeable or
      exceptional events, rather than routine departures from the norm such as seasonal
      heavy rainfall, seasonal fluctuations in the non-residential and/or tourist populations,
      or seasonal changes in local economic activity.

2.102 Spill performance of a WWTW or network asset is an important factor in assessing
      compliance. We consider that companies should treat 20 spills per year as a material

                                           on Thames Water

       indicator of a breach which requires further investigation. This is equivalent to
       approximately one spill every two and a half weeks, which we consider is reasonably
       construed as routine spilling (that is, non-exceptional). Although this is not a binding
       threshold for compliance, as previously explained, we note that this threshold has
       been a rule of thumb used by the European Commission. Any number of spills below 20
       per year may still amount to a breach, in particular where there is an indication or
       evidence of related environmental harm for which there is an available BTKNEEC
       remedy. It is also possible that an asset spilling more than 20 times per year could, on
       investigation, be found to be compliant, for example because of exceptional
       circumstances or because of the application of the BTKNEEC test. Each potential
       breach must be assessed on a case-by-case basis.

2.103 Therefore, as a minimum, if an asset spills 20 or more times per year, in accordance
      with a company's obligation under Regulation 4 UWWTR to "ensure" asset compliance,
      we expect a company to further assess that asset's compliance with Regulation 4
      UWWTR. This would involve: (i) identifying the cause of and circumstances relevant to
      the spills (and whether or not the spills have in fact occurred due to exceptional
      circumstances); and (ii) determining their impact on the environment and whether
      there are improvements consistent with BTKNEEC that would reduce or remove any
      harm (which should then be implemented) or whether it would be disproportionately
      costly to do so. Where a company has been unable to provide evidence showing that
      there have been exceptional circumstances, no environmental harm or a BTKNEEC
      exception in relation to storm overflows having 20 or more spills a year, there is a
      strong likelihood that it is operating in breach of Regulation 4(2) or Regulation 4(4) in
      relation to collecting systems and WWTW respectively. In those circumstances, we
      would also consider that the company has failed in its overarching obligation to ensure
      that its assets are operating in compliance with Regulation 4(2) UWWTR.

2.104 We consider that storm overflows that are discharging 20 times or more where there is
      no evidence of exceptional circumstances and there is a BTKNEEC solution for any
      environmental harm which has not been implemented are clearly in breach of
      Regulation 4(2) UWWTR or Regulation 4(4) UWWTR. Similarly, we will consider the
      company to be in breach where it has identified that the discharges are caused by
      operational or maintenance repair issues, rather than hydraulic capacity issues, but
      these have not been resolved.

2.105 Further, reflecting paragraph 2.96 and 2.97 above, if a company cannot provide
      evidence that it has investigated apparent routine discharges as identified through
      spill data and taken appropriate remedial action where there were compliance issues
      in a timely way, or that it is now in the process of investigating such discharges with a
      view to ensuring compliance with Regulation 4 UWWTR, we will consider that company
      to have breached or to be in breach (respectively) of its obligations to ensure asset
      compliance under Regulation 4 UWWTR.

 3. Our investigation

 Background

3.1   On 18 November 2021, Ofwat and the Environment Agency announced investigations into
      all water and wastewater companies in England and Wales. This was prompted by
      companies revealing to the Storm Overflows Taskforce 61 that data from the installation of
      new EDM and flow measurement devices at their WWTW had indicated that they may not
      be complying with the FFT requirement in their environmental permits. As a result, some
      WWTW might not be treating as much sewage as they should be, which could be
      resulting in sewage discharges into storm tanks and/or the environment at times when
      this should not be happening.

3.2   On the same day, we wrote to all water and wastewater companies in England and Wales
      requesting that they provide a range of information to us. This included:

         •   Providing details about the number of WWTW the company had that might not be
             meeting the FFT requirements of their environmental permits, and an estimate of
             the discharges to the environment this might have caused;

         •   If this was happening, explaining the reasons why;

         •   Explaining how the company managed its WWTW to ensure they meet the FFT
             requirements of their environmental permits;

         •   Setting out what role their board plays in ensuring the company is meeting its FFT
             requirements;

         •   Describing how the company’s board considers the company’s environmental
             performance when making its decisions about the dividends and executive pay
             and bonuses the company pays out; and

         •   Setting out their plans and timelines to put right any problems uncovered.

3.3   We received responses from all companies in December 2021.

  Other indicators of potential permit non-compliance

3.51    As explained above, although our investigation initially focused on Thames Water's
        compliance with its FFT permit conditions and what this indicated for the obligations
        Ofwat is responsible for enforcing, the information provided by Thames Water revealed
        further issues in the way that the company constructs, operates, maintains and

        highlighted potential compliance concerns in relation to other aspects of the operation
        of its WWTW (which we consider relevant indicators of the UWWTR compliance). This
        included the ability of its WWTW to treat sewage within permit limits, which, at that
        time, Thames Water acknowledged was "becoming increasingly challenging due to
        population growth, headroom erosion and tightening consents". It also acknowledged

  Dry Weather Flow

3.54    Data obtained during the course of our investigation confirmed the deterioration in the
        company's DWF compliance position with an increasing number of sites failing to meet
        DWF permit conditions in at least one year and an increasing number of sites seeing an
        erosion in headroom and therefore at greater risk of failing.

3.55    As set out in Section 2, WWTW with DWF environmental permit conditions are expected
        to be able to treat the Q80 113 flow and companies are expected to monitor whether a site

        changes in weather from year to year means that it may not be possible for a WWTW to
        achieve the Q80 metric in each and every year, a prudent company should investigate
        any WWTW that fail to achieve Q80 to ensure that it understands why this is the case and

3.63   It is evident that sites that are operating with little or no headroom are at greater risk of

  Storm tank capacity

3.64   In addition to the evidence about Thames Water's deteriorating position in relation to
       DWF, data provided to us by the company also indicates a deteriorating position in
       relation to the capacity of other assets to deal with the increasing volumes of
       wastewater that they are required to do.

3.65   As indicated in Section 2, in our investigation we have benchmarked the storm tank
       provision to a volume equivalent of six hours of DWF for the WWTW. Storing less than this
       would mean spills to the environment will likely be higher than would otherwise be the
       case as a company may not have sufficient storage capacity to prevent short-term high
       flow levels from leading to discharges to the environment. This in turn could indicate
       that a company is failing to comply with the requirements of the UWWTR as it would not
       be minimising adverse impacts on the environment to at least the degree originally
       expected by its environmental permit.

3.66   In Thames Water's case, in addition to concerns about FFT compliance at 157 of its sites,
       and potential DWF issues at a growing number of sites, in its January 2023 response on
       its root cause analysis, it also identified potential issues with storm tank capacity at
       more than a third of its sites of concern (that is, 57 sites or 36% of the sites of concern).

3.67   Separately, Thames Water also provided data on storage capacity at a number of its
       WWTW (but was not able to do so for all sites). For the 193 sites for which information
       was provided, 62% had storage capacity of six hours or less of permit DWF limit and so,
       are at greater risk of breaching permit conditions and spilling to the environment.



  Potential non-compliance with wider environmental and
  regulatory obligations

3.68   As explained in Section 2, a company must ensure that discharges of untreated
       wastewater to the environment, either directly or via storm tanks, only occur in
       exceptional circumstances unless it can demonstrate that there was no environmental
       harm or that there is no BTKNEEC compatible remedial action it can take. Where a spill
       does occur, a company is expected to mitigate any harm to the environment resulting
       from it, again subject to BTKNEEC. We also explained that non-compliance with these

  The reasons for high spills from Thames Water's storm overflows

3.89    As explained in Section 2, there are circumstances in which a site which has recorded a
        high number of spills may still be considered to have complied with UWWTR
        requirements relating to discharges because, for example, the spill took place in
        exceptional circumstances, the spill did not result in environmental harm or the
        company is able to demonstrate that the high spilling site is subject to a BTKNEEC
        exception.

3.90    In the following section, therefore, we consider evidence on the extent to which these
        exceptions may have applied and the extent to which Thames Water has taken all the
        steps it is required to take to remediate high spilling sites in accordance with BTKNEEC.

3.91    Storm overflows which have spill levels above the SOAF thresholds are expected to be
        investigated by the companies. As explained in Section 2, Stage 1 of the SOAF requires a
        company to identify the reasons for the spills (and forms part of a company's annual
        return to the Environment Agency in addition to data on the number and duration of
        spill). These reasons fall into the following categories:

          •   Exceptional rainfall: This does not refer to individual rainfall events, but rather the
              rainfall across the reporting year.

          •   Asset Maintenance: Where the storm overflow and potentially parts of the
              upstream and downstream sewer network have not operated as
              designed/expected, high spill counts (over 60 times per year) can be caused". 148

          •   Hydraulic capacity: If the reason for a high spilling storm overflow (over 60 times
              per year) is neither “exceptional rainfall” nor “asset maintenance” then the reason
              is classified under the “Hydraulic capacity” category. This indicates there is
              insufficient capacity (conveyance or storage) in the sewer network to cope with
              the wastewater flow plus typical rainfall entering the sewer network.

3.92    As set out in Table 3.5, Thames Water has not identified exceptional rainfall as the
        reason for spills above the SOAF threshold at any of its high spilling sites over the period
        from 2021 to 2023. Instead, asset maintenance was identified as the reason for high
        spills at a significant number of its sites - over 60% of high spilling sites in 2021, 38.7%
        in 2022 and 40.4% in 2023.

  High spilling sites due to asset maintenance

3.93   Under the SOAF framework, if the cause of spills which was triggered under SOAF (for
       example, the site has recorded more than 60 spills in one year) is identified as being due
       to asset maintenance, the storm overflow is removed from the SOAF process at this
       Stage (Stage 1). The removal of these sites from the SOAF process reflects the fact that
       companies are expected to be able to resolve these issues within the calendar year as
       part of their ongoing operational and maintenance activities (activities that companies
       are already funded for under their price control base allowances).

3.94   The Environment Agency's published spills data would seem to indicate, however, that

   Pollution incidents

3.106    As set out in Section 2, in our view, we would expect that a reasonable company would
         have systems in place to enable it to have sufficient oversight of what is happening at its
         WWTW and on its network and the extent to which its assets are operating as they
         should do to minimise any adverse impact on the environment.

3.107    Thames Water has claimed that it was a lack of accurate data on what was happening
         across its network that impacted negatively on its ability to understand its compliance
         position. However, in our view, the data that was already available to Thames Water
         should have highlighted concerns about how its assets were operating and should have
         triggered more rigorous and urgent investigation. This is particularly so given the known
         compliance risks that the company was already aware of as a result of its G2G risk
         assessment and also, given the fact that the company had been the subject of previous
         enforcement action as a result of a series of serious pollution incidents arising from
         failings at its WWTW and on its network 158.

3.108    Despite these past prosecutions, Thames Water's performance in terms of pollution
         incidents has remained a cause of significant concern. In 2021, for example, it was
         downgraded from a 3* to a 2* rated company (that is, one that requires improvement)
         by the Environment Agency in its annual Environmental Performance Assessment
         (EPA) 159. Figures for 2022 and 2023 160 show that its environmental performance
         continued to be disappointing and it remained a 2* rated company.

        increased pollution incidents, Thames Water has also been the subject of significant and
        sustained criticism from several environmental non-governmental organisations
        (eNGOs) and community groups relating to the frequency and duration of spills of
        untreated sewage to local waterways and the company's alleged failure to invest
        adequately to cater for the growth in population in its region.

3.119   Citizen scientists and volunteers working with Windrush Against Sewage Pollution

        compliance issues and advocating for change. This has included collecting and
        analysing data on flow and sewage spills at Thames Water's sites over a number of years.

        Water and the Environment Agency using Environmental Information Regulation (EIR)

   Summary of evidence relating to the performance of the company's
   wastewater assets

3.127   As set out in the preceding sections, we have received and considered a range of
        evidence and information on the performance of Thames Water's WWTW and its
        wastewater network. This has revealed a number of concerns, across a range of different
        metrics and indicators that are relevant to understanding whether the company is
        complying with its legal obligations relating to discharges to the environment. In
        summary, the evidence shows that:

          •   Two thirds of all its WWTW with FFT permit conditions or TDC (157 sites) have been
              identified by Thames Water as sites of concern with respect to their permit
              compliance.

          •   88 of these sites were identified as clearly underperforming and appear to be
              incapable of meeting FFT permit conditions, while a further 69 sites, while having
              the capacity to meet FFT permit conditions, were not doing so on a consistent
              basis.

          •   Ten sites have failed to meet DWF permit conditions and Thames Water
              acknowledged that the number could increase to more than 20 by 2025 if issues
              are not addressed.

          •   A growing number of sites have already seen significant headroom erosion and are,
              therefore, at risk of failing to meet DWF conditions. This, in turn, increases the risk
              of unpermitted spills of untreated sewage from these sites.

          •   57 sites (or more than a third of its sites of concern) have been identified by
              Thames Water as having insufficient storage tank capacity, and over 60% of sites
              for which it was able to provide data had storage capacity of six hours or less of
              permit DWF limit. These sites are, therefore, at greater risk of breaching permit
              conditions and of unpermitted spills of untreated sewage.

          •   Thames Water has reported high number of spills from its storm overflows – but
              these numbers are likely to under-report the true scale of spills which have
              actually occurred across its wastewater network.

   Thames Water's processes and procedures for identifying and
   addressing compliance risks

3.128    Thames Water has highlighted the lack of accurate data as the main reason for its
         failure to identify compliance issues on the scale that it has now done. However, as
         outlined above, there were other indicators and sources of information which could
         have, and should have, alerted the company about the performance of its wastewater
         assets and the extent to which it was operating and maintaining these assets to ensure
         it was able to meet local demand and to minimise adverse effects on the environment,
         and hence to comply with its legal obligations to do so.

3.129    In this section we consider the processes and procedures that Thames Water has told us
         it had/has in place to enable it to identify and address compliance risks.

3.130    Outside of the G2G asset-wide risk assessments that Thames Water undertook in 2017
         and repeated in 2020, it told us that it also had various ad-hoc processes and
         procedures in place to enable it to assess FFT compliance and inform decisions with
         respects to the performance of its WWTW. These processes included site visits combined
         with remote monitoring of key assets, processes, and data. Thames Water claimed that
         these operational processes enabled it to ensure that any anomalies that might arise
         were flagged, investigated and rectified in a timely manner, or, if necessary, escalated
         or used to identify investment needs or additional funding to ensure that such issues did
         not occur in future.

3.131    Thames Water explained, for example, that all WWTW with storm discharge permits
         have had remote monitoring capability which include storm tank levels and key process
         assets. Alarms have been monitored centrally in Thames Water's Waste Operational
         Control Room which has been manned 24/7. Site processes have been audited by
         process scientists with data from larger sites being collated centrally and reviewed to

       As part of the price review process Ofwat sets performance commitments to incentivise companies
   to deliver on the outcomes that matter to their customers and the environment. Performance
   commitments have either financial or reputational incentives (‘Outcome Delivery Incentives (ODIs)’)
   associated with them. The majority of these incentives are financial which means that if a company
   performs better than the performance commitment level, it may get an outperformance payment
   (which means that it recovers more revenue from customers) and if it performs below the commitment
   level it may have to make an underperformance payment (which means that customers pay less). In
   this way, each company’s management and its investors are encouraged to deliver what customers
   want. They incur outperformance payments for doing better than their performance commitment
   target; and underperformance payments if fail to meet those targets. The underperformance payments
   incurred by companies for not meeting performance levels set at a price review are distinct from
   enforcement penalties that Ofwat may impose under section 22A of the WIA91. The former is part of
   mechanisms used at price reviews to incentivise good performance and the achievement of agreed
   performance standards; the latter are penalties for breaching enforceable statutory or licence
   requirements.
   All water companies in England and Wales are also required to publish information about their
   performance in an Annual Performance Report. This includes information about how they have done in
   meeting their performance commitments; whether they have earned any out or underperformance
   payments for their delivery against these commitments; and if companies are failing to deliver, how
   they will put things right.

4. Our assessment and findings

Introduction and overview
4.1   As required by section 22A(6) of the WIA91, we set out the statutory provisions and
      relevant licence conditions that we consider Thames Water has breached and explain
      our assessment of the evidence we have considered in reaching our conclusion. We
      have also taken account of the responses that we received to the consultation on our
      draft decision.

4.2   For the reasons set out further below, we are satisfied that, from at least 2017, Thames
      Water has contravened Regulations 4(4)(a) and Regulation 4(2) and Schedule 2
      UWWTR by failing to ensure that its WWTW and collecting systems are designed,
      constructed, operated and maintained adequately according to the standards and
      requirements set out in these regulations. These breach are in themselves breaches of
      section 94 WIA91.

4.3   The magnitude and extent of Thames Water’s contraventions of the UWWTR is
      significant, widespread and has persisted over an extended period. Accordingly, we
      are satisfied that in addition to these UWWTR breaches, this indicates a systemic
      failure by the company to make appropriate provision for effectually providing
      drainage and dealing with the contents of sewers and, therefore, itself constitutes a
      breach of section 94 WIA91.

4.4   We are also satisfied that, from at least 2017, Thames Water has contravened
      paragraph 12 of Condition P by failing to ensure it had adequate financial and
      management resources and systems of planning and internal control in place to carry
      out its regulated activities and, in particular, to manage and operate its WWTW to
      ensure compliance with UWWTR and section 94 WIA91.

4.5   As outlined in Section 3, this view has been reached following a lengthy investigation
      during which we made multiple detailed requests for information and data to Thames
      Water. In addition to the hundreds of documents provided by the company, we
      reviewed environmental performance and spills data published by the Environment
      Agency and considered relevant information provided to Ofwat by stakeholders,
      including eNGOs, in Thames Water's area. We have also taken into account the
      responses that we received to the consultation on our draft decision.

4.6   As noted previously, our investigation broadened from issues related to FFT to wider
      concerns about Thames Water's management of its wastewater treatment network as
      more evidence was uncovered. This evidence has revealed a failure by the company to
      have a clear view or understanding about the state of its wastewater assets (including
      the actual number of storm overflows on its network); about how its assets were

4.7    In the following sections, we consider each of the statutory provisions and relevant
       licence conditions that we consider Thames Water has breached.

Findings in relation to a breach of the UWWTR
4.8    As set out in Section 2, Regulation 4 UWWTR requires a water company to ensure that
       its WWTW plants are designed, constructed, operated and maintained to ensure that
       spills only occur in exceptional or unforeseeable circumstances in all local climatic
       conditions, subject to the BTKNEEC test. As explained previously, we have considered
       both the extent to which:

           a) the company's assets comply with the requirements of Regulation 4 UWWTR
              (that is, in terms of whether they are providing sufficient performance), and

           b) the extent to which the company has met its obligation under Regulation 4
              UWWTR to ensure that its assets continue to meet the relevant standards (that
              is, how it has gone about ensuring that they provide sufficient performance).

4.9    While Ofwat is not responsible for assessing and enforcing breaches of environmental
       permits, non-compliance with the conditions of those permits is a strong indicator
       that duties under Regulation 4 UWWTR are not being met, as it might point to the
       asset no longer having the capacity to meet sufficient performance or to inadequate
       operation and maintenance of the asset to enable sufficient performance. These are
       not the only indicators we have looked at, however, and compliance with a permit does
       not necessarily equal compliance with the requirements of Regulation 4.

4.12   Thames Water has sought to argue that as it has now determined that 48 of its 157
       sites of concern serve agglomerations with a population equivalent of less than
       2,000 231, that these sites should be excluded from the scope of our investigation and

       we have explained previously, while Regulation 4(2) imposes obligations in respect of
       the provision of collecting systems “for every agglomeration with a population
       equivalent of 2,000 or more”, Regulation 4(4) does apply to smaller agglomerations,
       because, (i) the obligation is to ensure that water is, before discharge, “subject to
       treatment provided in accordance with regulation 5”, and (ii) although regulation 5
       imposes specific obligations as regards the treatment plants that must be in place in
       respect of larger agglomerations, it also requires “appropriate treatment” of water
       from agglomerations of less than 2,000. In our view, therefore, all 157 of Thames
       Water's WWTW which it has identified as sites of concern are also covered by
       Regulation 4(4).

Failure to limit discharges from storm overflows at WWTW

4.27      As discussed in Section 2, the purpose of the UWWTR is to ensure that under all
          normal weather conditions, the wastewater collected by a catchment area's sewer
          system is treated to a required standard before discharge. Untreated discharges to
          the environment should therefore only occur in exceptional circumstances or where
          the costs of reducing harm are disproportionate to the environmental benefit that
          would be gained (the BTKNEEC test), and companies should minimise any adverse
          impacts to the environment arising from these discharges.

4.28      We consider that companies should treat 20 spills per year as a material indicator of a
          breach of Regulation 4 UWWTR which requires further investigation to ensure
          compliance. In the absence of the relevant evidence that there has been exceptional
          circumstances, that no environmental harm has arisen or a BTKNEEC exception exists,
          we will consider storm overflows having 20 or more spills a year as evidence that they
          are probably in breach of Regulation 4 UWWTR. We consider that storm overflows that
          are discharging 20 times or more, where there is no evidence of exceptional
          circumstances, and it is clear there is a BTKNEEC solution (including operational
          solutions) which has not been implemented are clearly in breach of Regulation 4
          UWWTR. Likewise if a company cannot evidence that it has investigated apparent
          routine discharges and taken appropriate remedial action in a timely way, or is in the
          process of investigating such, we consider a company to have breached or to be in
          breach of Regulation 4.

4.30   Absent evidence of exceptional circumstances or a BTKNEEC exemption, the fact that
       storm overflows at the WWTW in question are being used so regularly would indicate
