Sites spilling frequently due to asset maintenance issues

4.33   For sites triggered for investigation under SOAF, where the root cause of high spills
       was identified as being operational and maintenance (asset maintenance) issues, we
       have taken this into account in our penalty assessment if the cause of the spill has not
       been rectified within the calendar year (as is required under SOAF) so that it
       continues to record high spills in the following year. For example, for sites which
       spilled more than 60 times in 2021 due to asset maintenance reasons we consider that
       site to have not only breached UWWTR but have also included in in our penalty
       assessment if that site also spilled 20 or more times in 2022 as this indicates that the
       cause of the spill has not been resolved as is required under SOAF.

4.34   As noted in Section 3, over 60% of Thames Water's sites were which were triggered for
       investigation under SOAF in 2021 (that is, had spilled more than 60 times) were found
       to have done so because of asset maintenance issues. Similarly, 63% of all the sites
       that Thames Water had told us it had assessed as part of the SOAF process, did not
       progress beyond Stage 1 as they were found to be due to asset maintenance and
       operational issues. The fact that spills at so many of the company's highest spilling
       sites are due to asset maintenance issues is concerning. In our view, a company
       should be able to operate and manage its assets to prevent issues occurring in the
       first place. Spills due to asset maintenance issues should be the exception and not, as
       appears to be the case with Thames Water, the norm.

4.35   Furthermore, if and when a site has recorded high spill numbers due to asset
       maintenance reasons, we would expect the company to act swiftly to resolve those
       issues to prevent the site also recording high spills in subsequent periods: where
       there is an available operational or maintenance fix, carrying out that work would
       almost inevitably constitute a viable BTKNEEC solution, in which case the failure to
       carry out the work would constitute a breach of Regulation 4(4). It appears that
       Thames Water has failed to carry out such operational and maintenance fixes in
       relation to several of its assets with the result that a significant number of sites which
       had spilled more than 60 times in 2021 continued to record 20 or more spills in 2022.

Thames Water's failure to act to ensure its wastewater assets are

4.59   As already explained above, Regulation 4 UWWTR not only sets out the requirements
       for the design, construction, maintenance and operation of wastewater assets (with
       the underlying goal of preventing environmental harm), but also requires the
       companies to ensure that its assets are UWWTR compliant.

4.60   The scale and duration of potential non-compliance that our investigation has found
       at so many of Thames Water's sites, and across so many aspects of its operation and
       management of its wastewater infrastructure, is extremely concerning.

4.61   This is particularly so given the fact that the company was already aware of the
       consequences of failing to operate its assets to meet environmental permit conditions
       and the impact that these failings can have on the environment. As noted in Section 3,
       in 2017 Thames Water was fined £20.3 million by the Environment Agency as a result of
       serious and prolonged pollution incidents on the river Thames due to unpermitted
       discharges of untreated sewage from its WWTW. The company's failure to manage its
       FFT compliance was a key aspect of those prosecutions.

4.62   Following those prosecutions, and engagement with the Environment Agency, in 2017
       Thames Water undertook an estate-wide assessment of its compliance risks. While
       this focused primarily on FFT compliance, it also considered a number of other metrics
       (which are relevant indicators of UWWTR compliance) to reflect asset health, as well
       as factors such as the sensitivity of the watercourse that the WWTW was discharging
       into. While this assessment had rated more than 100 sites as red or amber in terms of
       potential compliance risks, Thames Water chose to prioritise action at fewer than 30 of
       these under its G2G programme. This also meant that the bulk of its WWTW, which it
       knew had compliance risks or which were at heightened risk of non-compliance, were
       not prioritised for resolution and so, were not addressed with any urgency.

Section 94 WIA91: Failure to effectually deal with the contents of sewers

4.69   As explained in Section 2, each breach of Regulation 4 UWWTR itself constitutes a
       breach of section 94 WIA91. However, in addition to the UWWTR breaches identified
       above, we have also considered whether the company has breached its general duties
       under section 94 WIA91. The magnitude and extent of Thames Water’s contraventions
       of the UWWTR is significant, widespread and has persisted over an extended period.
       Accordingly, we are satisfied that this indicates a systemic failure to make appropriate
       provision for effectually dealing with the contents of sewers and, therefore,
       constitutes a breach of the general duty under section 94 WIA91.

4.70   In coming to this conclusion, we have relied on the following conduct:

        •   Thames Water identified 157 potentially FFT non-compliant sites. This equates to
            almost two thirds of all its sites which have FFT permit conditions or TDCs. Of
            these sites, Thames Water’s analysis demonstrated that virtually all of these
            potentially non-compliant sites have multiple root causes for failing FFT
            performance, including data quality issues, poor flow control and management,
            and lack of treatment resilience such as inadequate maintenance or the capacity
            of assets no longer being sufficient to meet local demand. In addition, Thames
            Water identified issues with storm tank capacity at more than a third of its sites
            of concern as well as an increasing number of sites which had failed, or were at
            risk of failing, to meet DWF permit conditions. In our assessment, this is
            representative of a widespread and persistent failure to meet Thames Water’s
            obligations under Regulation 4(4) UWWTR.

        •   The magnitude and duration of spills from storm overflows associated with its
            WWTW, the majority of which appear to be due to operational and asset
            maintenance issues which should be within Thames Water's control, also point to
            a breach of the company's obligations under Regulation 4(4) UWWTR. In 2021, for
            example, over 70% of storm overflows associated with its WWTW had spilled 20 or
            more times. While recognising the steps that Thames Water has taken at its high
            spilling sites under the SOAF process, our overall assessment is that Thames

            scale failure by the company to ensure its wastewater assets are managed,

        •   Thames Water continued to operate with the knowledge that failing to prioritise

            the sites with a red or amber rating under the original 2017 G2G assessment are
            sites which were also rated red or amber when the company repeated its G2G risk
            assessment in 2020 and are also sites which are amongst Thames Water's 157
            sites of concern. These issues were clearly widespread, and the evidence
            available to us indicates that Thames Water persistently failed to ensure that its
            WWTW met its UWWTR obligations and its obligations under section 94 WIA91.

4.71   In summary, therefore, based on the evidence obtained during the course of our
       investigation, and for the reasons outlined above, we have concluded that, from at
       least 2017, Thames Water failed, and continues to fail, to comply with its obligations
       under Regulation 4(4), Regulations 4(2) and Schedule 2 of the UWWTR and its duties
       under section 94 WIA91.

4.72   While Thames Water has acknowledged that, historically, its processes and
       governance arrangement could have been better, to date, it has not acknowledged
       that the scale and duration of compliance issues across its WWTW estate (and the
       likely impact that this non-compliance has had on the environment) constitutes a
       breach of its duties under the UWWTR and section 94 WIA91.

4.73   We have considered Thames Water's response to our draft decision and have taken
       account of the new information and evidence it has provided. However, in reaching
       our findings in relation to the extent to which the company has complied, and
       continues to comply with, its obligations under section 94, we have based our
       assessment on the magnitude and extent of Thames Water's potential non-compliance
       in relation to FFT permit conditions; the evidence on the increasing number of its sites
       which have failed (or are at risk of failing) to meet DWF permit conditions as well as
       the significant number of its sites that are spilling to the environment frequently. In
       our view, this evidence points to a systemic failure to make appropriate provision for
       effectually dealing with the contents of sewers and constitutes an ongoing breach of
       section 94 WIA91.

4.74   We also consider that, despite Thames Water's repeated claims to the contrary, it has
       not behaved in a manner we would expect of a reasonable company. In our view, it
       should have been aware of, and alert to, the risk that a failure to meet FFT and other
       permit conditions and its spills and pollution incidents performance might mean for
       the company's wider regulatory obligations. Not only had the company been the
       subject of previous prosecutions due to the environmental impact of the failure of a
       number of its sites to treat sufficient FFT, but it was also aware of, and had considered,
       the implications for the company as a result of Ofwat's decision in the Southern Water
       enforcement case. In doing so, it had identified a number of risks which it failed to
       address with sufficient urgency. As a result of those failures, and despite the fact that
       companies were funded to meet existing environmental permits under the price
       control, Thames Water is now in a position where almost two thirds of all its sites with
       FFT permit conditions and TDCs are potentially non-compliant. This means that sites
       may have been discharging untreated wastewater when they should not be doing so
       and, in circumstances which were not due to exceptional or unforeseeable events.

Findings in respect of Condition P: Failure to have adequate financial
and management resources and systems of planning and internal
control to enable it to secure the carrying out of its regulated activities

4.75   The breaches we have identified above demonstrate that Thames Water has failed to
       properly carry out its regulated activities, in particular, to design, construct, operate
       and maintain its WWTW and the collecting systems that supply its WWTW in order to
       minimise harm to the environment. We consider that this is due to the failures in, and
       the inadequacy of, the financial and management resources and systems of planning
       and internal controls that it put towards these regulated activities, contrary to the
       company's obligations under Condition P of its Licence (as explained in Section 2).

4.76   Condition P means that Thames Water needs to have understood its legal and
       regulatory obligations and have put in place appropriate processes and controls to
       ensure that it was able to operate its wastewater assets in a manner that complied
       with those obligations.

4.77   It should also have in place systems to ensure that any non-compliance (and the risk
       of non-compliance) is escalated within the company and that prompt, timely
       investigations are carried out and remedial action taken to secure compliance. It
       should also have internal controls in place that follow-up these interventions to ensure
       that compliance is achieved in a timely and effective manner.

4.78   Thames Water should have in place appropriate processes to ensure that its
       operational staff have the necessary information to identify potential issues and that it
       has the right culture and processes in place to ensure that remediation of these issues
       is prioritised. This includes making sure that it has appropriate checks and balances
       to assure monitoring and reporting information is accurate. Thames Water should also

       have in place processes to ensure that its Executive and Board request and receive the
       information they need to monitor the company's compliance with its environmental

4.79   Based on the evidence we have seen, we have concluded that Thames Water has had:

       •   inadequate systems of planning and internal controls and management resources

           UWWTR / section 94) at its WTTW and on its network;

       •   inadequate financial and management resources in place to adequately ensure
           that its WWTW and its network continue to be designed, constructed, operated and
           maintained to meet local conditions, and that solutions to non-compliance are
           identified and addressed in a timely way; and

       •   inadequate processes of assurance, controls and governance to ensure and
           challenge the completeness and integrity of WWTW and network asset compliance
           reporting, including at Board and Executive level.

4.80   As set out in Section 3, during the course of our investigation, Thames Water identified
       more and more sites which were potentially non-compliant with their FFT permit
       conditions. This was despite the previous compliance risk assessments that the
       company had undertaken under its G2G programme and despite the robust processes
       and procedures that it claimed to have had in place to identify and manage its

4.81   When asked to provide an explanation or root cause of what had gone wrong to result
       in the company ending up with potential FFT non-compliance on the scale it has now
       identified, Thames Water repeatedly cited a lack of accurate data. It told us that this
       will be resolved by the roll-out of U_MON3 and U_MON4 monitors and this will improve
       its ability to manage compliance across its WWTW estate.

4.82   However, the duties and obligations imposed on companies by the UWWTR and section
       94 WIA91 have existed for many years and the onus is, and always has been, on the
       company to ensure its compliance with these obligations. How it does that, and the
       processes and procedures it has in place, to assure itself that it is complying is up to
       the company. The absence of data from U_MON3 and U_MON4 monitors does not
       explain (or excuse) how, and why, Thames Water has ended up with so many
       potentially non-compliant sites. Rather, the scale of the potential non-compliance
       now identified points to a failure of the company's systems of planning and control to
       enable it to assure itself of its actual compliance position and a failure by the company

5. Our decision to issue an enforcement order

Background
5.1       Under section 18 WIA91, if we are satisfied that a regulated company is contravening
          or likely to contravene a condition of its Licence or a statutory requirement we are
          under the duty to make an enforcement order containing such provisions as are
          requisite to secure compliance with that condition or requirement.

5.2       Under section 19 WIA91, we are not required to make an enforcement order if we are
          satisfied that the contravention in question is of a trivial nature, or is contrary to our
          duties in Part I WIA91, including our duty to have regard to best regulatory practice
          and our other duties under section 2 WIA91. We may also instead or in part accept
          formal undertakings from a company to take remedial steps as long as we consider
          them appropriate to secure compliance. A company's obligation to comply with an
          undertaking is treated as a statutory requirement which is enforceable by Ofwat under
          section 18 WIA91.

5.3       We do not consider that any of the exceptions in section 19 WIA91 apply and we are
          therefore under a duty to make an enforcement order in this case. The breaches
          identified are significant. We are disappointed that Thames Water has not offered
          formal undertakings which would displace our duty to make an enforcement order. In
          making this decision, we have taken account of Thames Water's financial and
          operational issues alongside our section 2 WIA91 duties more generally including the
          interests of customers and the environment in a restoration of compliance as quickly
          and efficiently as reasonably possible. Our enforcement order is specifically designed
          to take account of issues of affordability, deliverability and financeability in the steps
          and timescales for delivering compliance.

5.4       Under section 108 of the Deregulation Act 2014, in carrying out our enforcement duty
          under section 18 WIA we must have regard to the desirability of promoting economic
          growth, and in particular in a way which ensures that regulatory action is only taken
          where needed; and any action is proportionate. We are also required to have regard to
          any guidance that the secretary of state may issue in relation to the application of this
          duty.

5.5       We note that in the introduction to the duty 274 the current guidance states that the
          duty does not legitimise non-compliance with other duties or objectives, and its
          purpose is not to achieve or pursue economic growth at the expense of necessary
          protections. We also note that it recognises that enforcement action can be necessary
          to protect public health or the environment although care should be taken in relation

The enforcement order in this case

6. Our decision to impose a financial penalty and the
broad level of that penalty

Relevant provisions of the WIA91
6.1    Under sections 22A(1)(a) and 22A(2)(a) of the WIA91, Ofwat may impose on a water or
       sewerage company a penalty of such amount (not exceeding 10% of the regulated
       company's relevant turnover in a relevant year) as is reasonable in all the
       circumstances of the case, where it is satisfied that the company has contravened or
       is contravening any condition of its Licence, or any statutory requirement Ofwat is
       responsible for enforcing.

6.2    Under section 22A(11) of the WIA91, no penalty imposed by Ofwat under section 22A
       may exceed 10% of the turnover of the company, determined in accordance with the
       Water Industry (Determination of Turnover for Penalties) Order 2005. Article 3 of that
       Order provides that for the purposes of section 22A(11) of the WIA91, the relevant
       turnover of a company is the applicable turnover for the preceding business year net
       of tax (that is, the last business year preceding the date on which Ofwat gives notice
       under section 22A(6) of the WIA91). Article 2(2) defines “applicable turnover" as “the
       amounts, determined in conformity with normal accounting practice in the United
       Kingdom, which are derived by a company from the provision of goods and services in
       the course of the company's regulated activities in respect of which the penalty is
       imposed” and Article 2(1) defines “regulated activities" as:

               “(a) in the case of a company holding an appointment as a water undertaker,
               its functions as a water undertaker;

               (b) in the case of a company holding an appointment as a sewerage
               undertaker, its functions as a sewerage undertaker;”

6.3    For the purposes of the penalty in this case we have considered the business year from
       1 April 2023 to 31 March 2024. Thames Water's applicable turnover derived from its
       activities as a sewerage company in that business year was £1,160.998 million. 275
       Accordingly, the maximum penalty that we could impose on the company would be
       10% of this number, that is, £116.10 million.

The seriousness and duration of the contraventions

6.12   Thames Water must provide sewerage services across its area of appointment in line
       with its statutory duties and licence obligations. Under the UWWTR it is required to
       ensure that its WWTW are designed, constructed, operated and maintained in
       accordance with BTKNEEC so that, under normal local climatic conditions, all
       wastewater is collected and treated sufficiently in order to minimise adverse effects
       on the environment. As a general duty, section 94 WIA91 is one of the core obligations
       of a sewerage company. Condition P is a fundamental requirement of an efficient and
       effectively operated company. We therefore consider a contravention of these
       provisions to be serious.

6.13   In considering whether breaches of the UWWTR are sufficiently serious to warrant a
       penalty, we have focused on those breaches which are also inconsistent with the
       environmental permitting regime, or which involve assets spilling above the 60-spill
       SOAF threshold, and have also considered how Thames Water has engaged with the
       expectations of the SOAF.

6.14   We note, for example, that, in relation to breaches of Regulation 4(4) Thames Water
       recorded over 60 spills at almost 30% of the storm overflows associated with its WWTW
       in 2021 which surpasses the SOAF spill thresholds. At the same time, however, we also

       recognise that the company has engaged with the SOAF process and is in the process
       of completing, or has completed, investigations to identify and address potential root
       causes of spills at a significant number of sites where infiltration or hydraulic capacity
       have been identified as the reason for the high spills. We have taken this into account
       as part of our overall assessment of whether the company has breached its obligations
       in this case, including its obligations under UWWTR, and whether a breach is
       sufficiently serious to warrant the imposition of a penalty in this case.

6.15   We also note, however, that a significant number of the spills at Thames Water's high
       spilling sites have been due to asset maintenance issues (other than infiltration), such
       that (absent unusual circumstances) a BTKNEEC solution for the spill, that is, the
       proper maintenance of the existing assets, was readily available. In our assessment,
       these are issues that a diligent and reasonable company should be taking proactive
       steps to prevent and, if issues still arise, should be taking urgent remedial action to
       address.

6.16   On balance, therefore, and given the range of other factors that we considered when
       arriving at our decision, we remain of the view that Thames Water's has breached
       Regulation 4(4) and Regulation 4(2) of UWWTR, Section 94 WIA91 and Condition P of its
       licence. We also consider that nature and scale of these breaches warrant a
       significant penalty.

6.17   We also note that, despite the Board's awareness of issues at its WWTW and on its
       network and shortcomings in its compliance regime, it continued until relatively
       recently to assure us about the adequacy of its resources and systems of planning and
       internal control in the annual Ring-Fencing Certificate (RFC) and Risk and Compliance

6.18   We are satisfied that the breaches identified in this investigation occurred from at
       least March 2017 onwards. Thames Water has been aware of potential compliance

       G2G programme following prosecution by the Environment Agency. While we cannot

       storm overflows on the network, the evidence shows that a number of WWTW sites

Any damage caused to the environment

6.27   The evidence available to us indicates that Thames Water has persistently failed to
       ensure that its WWTW and networks are designed, constructed, operated and
       maintained so that, under the normal local climatic conditions, all wastewater is
       collected and treated sufficiently in order to minimise adverse effects on the
       environment.

6.28   As set out in Section 3, the poor performance and management of so many of Thames
       Water's WWTW and its failure to have proper oversight of storm overflows on its
       network has meant that spills of untreated wastewater have occurred in
       circumstances which could not be classed as exceptional. In 2021, for example, 73% of
       the storm overflows associated with Thames Water's WWTW (171 overflows) recorded
       20 or more spills and almost 30% recorded more than 60 spills (the majority of which
       due to asset maintenance issues). In addition, while the number of recorded spills
       from storm overflows on Thames Water's network were lower, the fact that in its return
       to the Environment Agency for 2022 it identified 312 additional storm overflows (the
       vast majority on its network) which had not previously been listed; which did not have
       monitors in place; and a significant number of which were also unpermitted 281 –
       suggests that the true scale of spills from Thames Water's storm overflows is likely to
       be much higher. While Thames Water has now told us that as a result of its
       investigations, it now believes that the number of 'genuine' overflows is lower than
       originally estimated, and that it has already applied for permits for a number of those
       overflows, the fact remains that Thames Water failed to ensure that all its assets are
       appropriately managed and monitored to meet the relevant standards and provide
       sufficient performance to comply with the UWWTR.

       of the sites which progressed to Stage 2 of the SOAF, the spills had had an

Whether the contravention or possibility of a contravention would have
been apparent to a diligent company

6.31   Thames Water’s poor performance has resulted, at least in part, from the
       shortcomings in the internal controls and management of its WWTW and network,
       which we consider would have been apparent to a diligent company. Moreover, even
       when the company was aware of actual non-compliance with environmental permits
       or the risk of non-compliance, it failed to act with sufficient urgency.

6.32   While Thames Water has repeatedly told us that its inability to identify potential non-
       compliance on the scale it now has is due, primarily, to a lack of accurate data, that
       lack of data in itself was due in part to its own failings to properly install and maintain
       EDM monitors at its WWTW (which in turn was failings to properly oversee its capital
       delivery partners). Regardless of the absence of data from monitors on its sites,
       Thames Water's processes and controls should have been robust enough to ensure
       that it had a full understanding of its assets and how those assets were performing –
       particularly given the fact that other sources of information, including mounting
       complaints from stakeholders, was clearly suggesting that things might be going
       wrong across is WWTW estate and network.

6.33   Instead of focusing on its true compliance position, the management and Board of
       Thames Water concentrated on a relatively narrow set of indicators or parameters
       which fed into the company's EPA report or were relevant to the company's PCs and
       ODIs. As a result, and despite the fact that this narrow focus was highlighted as a risk
       in its own internal reviews, there was a lack of sufficient challenge applied to WWTW
       and network performance and compliance information at Board level.

6.34   Thames Water remains ultimately responsible for ensuring that it has met its
       obligations. Given the scale of the potential non-compliance that Thames Water has
       reported and the frequency with which so many of its storm overflows were spilling,
       Ofwat considers that Thames Water did not have appropriate systems in place to
       enable it to identify and address potential non-compliance across its WWTW estate

6.37      In 2018 Ofwat also imposed a financial penalty on Thames Water itself for a failure to
          meet its obligations under section 37 WIA91 (the equivalent of its general duty under
          section 94 WIA91 but relating to the provision of water services) and Condition F (now
          Condition P).283 As a result of our case, Thames Water agreed formal undertakings
          under section 19 WIA91, which included undertakings regarding the adequacy of its
          systems of planning and control to meet its regulatory obligations.

6.38      The failings of Thames Water identified in this investigation, occurred despite the
          existence of these precedents. This further shows that Thames Water did not act like a
          diligent company.

Precedents set under equivalent provisions for other utilities

6.39      We are not aware of any relevant precedent decisions by other regulators in respect of
          provisions equivalent to the UWWTR, section 94 of the WIA91 and Condition P.

Conclusion on the appropriateness of financial penalty and its broad
level

6.40   Having considered the factors above, we are satisfied that a financial penalty is
       appropriate in Thames Water's case. As discussed in detail, we have found that
       Thames Water contravened several of its duties and obligations. These are interrelated
       to an extent and their combined effect impacts on the seriousness of Thames Water's
       conduct as a whole. Therefore, we consider it appropriate to issue a single penalty,
       rather than separate penalties in respect of each breach. The broad framework that
       we have used to assess the seriousness of the breaches we have identified, to
       establish the appropriate level of penalty is set out in Appendix A7.

6.41   In setting the broad penalty level, we took the factors above into account, as well as
       both the cumulative effect of all breaches and the degree of overlap between them.
       We have had particular regard to the serious and widespread nature of the breaches.

6.42   Against this background, therefore, we consider that the broad level of penalty should
       be set at 8.5% of the company's relevant turnover from its wastewater activities.



Aggravating and mitigating factors

6.43   As set out in our Statement of Policy, other aggravating and mitigating factors may be
       taken into consideration to make further adjustments to the penalty level. We are
       satisfied that certain further adjustments are warranted in Thames Water's case. We
       explain this in detail below in relation to the following factors we have considered:

            •   repeated contraventions or failures;
            •   the continuation of a contravention or failure;
            •   any involvement of senior management;
            •   the level of cooperation with any investigation carried out;
            •   any attempts to conceal the contravention or failure;
            •   the proactive reporting of the contravention or failure to the enforcement
                authority;
            •   taking appropriate action to acknowledge and rectify the contravention or
                failure; and
            •   activities to provide restitution and compensation.

Aggravating factors

Repeated contraventions or failures

6.44   Ofwat has not previously taken enforcement action against Thames Water under the
       UWWTR so the breaches of Regulation 4(4)(a) and Regulation 4(2) and Schedule 2 of
       the UWWTR identified in this investigation do not amount to repeated breaches.

6.45   In 2018, however, we found that Thames Water had breached section 37 WIA91 (an
       equivalent of section 94 WIA91 but for water) and Condition F (now Condition P) of its
       Licence. In this case, we have also concluded that the company has breached its
       obligations under Condition P. We appreciate that the breaches in the 2018 case and
       this investigation relate to different types of conduct by Thames Water and, to an
       extent, different obligations. However, the underlying issues surrounding the
       adequacy of Thames Water's financial and management resources and systems of
       planning and control to ensure it is able to fulfil its statutory obligations which gave
       rise to the breach of Condition P are similar in nature in both cases, and have also
       contributed to this breach. We therefore consider this to be an aggravating factor in
       determining an appropriate penalty level.

The continuation of a breach

6.46   As set out above, while we have previously taken enforcement action against the
       company in respect of a breach of its Licence condition (now Condition P), we have
       considered this as a repeated breach rather than a continuation of a previous breach
       in our assessment of potentially aggravating factors.

6.47   As we have not taken enforcement action against Thames Water previously for a
       breach of UWWTR so our findings in relation to Regulation 4(4)(a) and Regulation 4(2)
       and Schedule 2 UWWTR are not considered to be a continuation of a breach and
       therefore have not factored in our determination of an appropriate penalty level.

Any involvement of senior management

6.48   The company's senior management and Board were aware of at least some of the
       compliance risks at Thames Water's WWTW and failed to act to address those risks
       with sufficient urgency (even when the initial impetus for the company to undertake
       the compliance risk assessment was the fact that it had been the subject of a record
       fine for a number of serious pollution incidents at its WWTW and where a failure to
       manage its FFT permit compliance had been identified as a critical factor). The
       company also chose to defer investment on addressing known compliance risks and
       focus resources on areas which, it acknowledges, were, historically, subject to greater
       regulatory scrutiny.



                                                177
        Notice of Ofwat’s decision to issue an enforcement order and impose a financial penalty
                                           on Thames Water

6.49   It is also evident from the company's own internal audit reports that management had
       been alerted to the risks arising from the company's historic focus on metrics such as
       "end of pipe" compliance rather than on how the company's WWTW were being
       managed in terms of flow compliance and what this might mean for the company's
       compliance regime. These reports also highlighted issues with the company's
       systems, processes and reporting arrangement. Despite this, and despite the fact that
       Thames Water already had section 19 undertaking in place which covered Condition P
       as a result of previous enforcement action we had taken against it, the senior
       management and Board failed to act to address these issues. We consider this to be an
       aggravating factor.

Any attempts to conceal the contravention or failure

6.50   While Thames Water has failed to identify and report the issues concerned in this
       investigation, we have seen no evidence that the company sought to deliberately
       conceal the contraventions or failures identified by our investigation. We therefore do
       not propose to make any adjustments to the penalty level in this respect.



Mitigating factors

The level of co-operation with any investigation carried out

6.51   In general, we expect the regulated companies to cooperate with our investigations. In
       the case of Thames Water, since the opening our investigation it has provided us with
       a large amount of material, shared with us the details of its own assessments and
       proactively engaged with us to identify the steps it might take to address the concerns
       identified. We note, however, that in some instances it failed to answer questions fully
       or chose to interpret our questions very narrowly. This meant that the case team had
       to issue further information requests, which in turn, added to the length of time of the
       information gathering phase of the investigation.

6.52   More specifically we acknowledge the cautious and inclusive approach Thames Water
       adopted in assessing the scale of potential non-compliance with FFT permit
       conditions. This meant that in addition to sites which are clearly underperforming, it
       also included sites where under-performance relative to FFT permit levels may have
       been marginal or skewed by a one-off event. On balance we consider this approach to
       be a mitigating factor in our determination of the penalty level.

The proactive reporting of the contravention or failure to the
enforcement authority

6.53   Thames Water has acknowledged that there have been historic failures of its
       processes in relation to its wastewater management and has also acknowledged the

                                                178
        Notice of Ofwat’s decision to issue an enforcement order and impose a financial penalty
                                           on Thames Water

       scale of its potential non-compliance with its environmental permits. It has also
       pointed to the significant steps that it is now takin to "rectify its accepted failings" 284,
       including proposing to invest over £1,044 million in AMP8 in wastewater compliance.
       However, it has not, to date, acknowledged that the failings identified during the
       course of our investigation, in turn, constitute breaches of the UWWTR, section 94
       WIA91 or Condition P. It has not been proactive in reporting these to Ofwat.

6.54   Indeed, the company has, until recently, continued to provide assurances to us, via its
       annual RFC and RCS, about the adequacy of its systems, processes and resources to
       enable it to meet its statutory and Licence obligations. We therefore do not propose to
       make any adjustments to the penalty level in this respect.

Taking appropriate action to acknowledge and rectify the contravention
or failure.

6.55   As above, Thames Water has not, to date, acknowledged that the issues identified in
       our investigation constitute breaches of the UWWTR, section 94 WIA91 or Condition P.
       However, as also highlighted above, it is now taking action to acknowledge and rectify
       its failings in relation to FFT permit conditions, DWF permit conditions and storm tank
       capacity issues. It has also engaged with the SOAF process and sought to investigate
       its high spilling storm overflows condition and to identify potential solutions at a
       significant number of these sites.

6.56   We also recognise that it has begun to take action to improve its processes and
       procedures to prevent similar issues arising in future and has also put new reporting
       structures in place to ensure a clearer line of sight between environmental permit
       compliance, the Executive and the Board. These steps are welcome. While it is not
       clear, at this stage, whether these steps will be sufficient to address all the issues
       identified as part of our investigation, we have, nevertheless, viewed this as a
       mitigating factor in relation to the determination of an appropriate penalty level.

Activities to provide restitution and compensation

6.57   Thames Water has not provided any assessment of the potential harm that its
       breaches may have caused. Whilst it has begun to take steps to improve engagement
       with local community groups and eNGOs to address their concerns and is seeking to
       be more transparent about the performance of its wastewater assets and the steps it
       is taking to improve that performance, we do not consider these steps to be sufficient
       to constitute a mitigating factor.

The penalty
6.58   Having considered each of the aggravating and mitigating factors outlined above, we
       have concluded that a further upward adjustment to the broad level starting point for
       the penalty is appropriate in this case, and that the final penalty level should be 9.0%
       of Thames Water's relevant turnover of £1,160.998 million. This is equivalent to a
       penalty of £104.5 million.

6.59   In reaching this decision, we have taken account of Thames Water's wider financial
       issues, but consider the fine to be proportionate within the context of Thames Water's
       compliance issues and its ability to finance its operations. Moreover, it is open to
       Thames Water to propose alternative payment terms for the financial penalty, that we
       must consider under section 22A(7) WIA91. We are disappointed that Thames Water
       has not proposed a settlement package that removes or reduces the need for this
       penalty and by providing suitable redress to customers and the environment.

Enforcement Order in relation to Thames Water

This document constitutes a final enforcement order (the Order) given by the Water Services
Regulation Authority (the Authority) to Thames Water Services Limited (the Licensee)
under section 18(1) of the Water Industry Act 1991, as amended (WIA91).

Except as otherwise provided in this Order, words and expressions used in this Order have the

On 28 May 2025, the Authority gave notice under section 20 WIA91 of its proposal to make an
order under section 18(1) WIA91 in relation to the Licensee (the 'Notice').

The purpose of this Order is to secure compliance by the Licensee with its statutory
obligations under Regulation 4 and Schedule 2 of the Urban Waste Water Treatment (England
and Wales) Regulations 1994 (UWWTR), section 94 WIA91, and its Instrument of Appointment
(the Licence).


As set out in the Notice:

•   The Licensee has contravened its statutory obligations by failing to ensure that its

agreement between the Licensee and the Authority, such agreement not to be unreasonably
withheld by the Authority or the Licensee in all circumstances.

Requirement 6: Reporting

The Licensee will report to us on a six-monthly basis on its progress against the requirements
of this Order and publish on its website details of its progress and a summary of the actions it
has taken. The first report should be provided by 5pm on 28 November 2025.

A failure to comply with this Order may result in the Authority seeking an injunction or other
forms of relief from the court or applying to the court for a special administration order
against the Licensee.

    Environment Agency. This is because the Environment Agency has a duty under

Our response

10. As we have explained in Section 2 of this document, Ofwat has a duty under section 18
    WIA to enforce Regulation 4(2) and 4(4) UWWTR as part of section 94 WIA. This duty is
    independent of the Environment Agency and Ofwat role in relation to the enforcement of,

    Environmental Permitting Regime (EPR). The Environment Agency is responsible for
    enforcing specific permit requirements under the EPR, whereas we are responsible for
    enforcing Regulation 4 UWWTR and section 94 WIA91.

11. We are aware of the Government's and the Environment Agency's existing policies and
    practices relating to wastewater discharges and permit compliance. We are also aware
    that the companies had, erroneously, believed the SOAF, in particular, to determine the
    limits of their compliance with UWWTR with respect to spills. Ofwat is the enforcing
    authority under Regulation 4 and 5 UWWTR, independent of the Environment Agency,
    which is primarily responsible for enforcing environmental permit requirements. Ofwat
    has a statutory duty to enforce the UWWTR, and companies have their own direct duties
    to comply with the UWWTR. In reaching our decision on penalties we have recognised
    that companies, erroneously, treated the SOAF and permitting regimes as the limit of
    their storm overflow remediation obligations, and only apply penalties where companies'
    failures go beyond these. Our approach is further detailed in Appendix A6. We have used
    our judgement to reflect the fact that the companies worked to a set of pre-existing
    policies, in particular the SOAF, which we took into account in setting the penalties. We

    P12.

12. Our final decision document sets out the approach we have taken to applying the

Approach to assessing spill compliance

15. All water companies, including Thames Water, told us that they do not recognise our
    interpretation of the UWWTR and disagreed with what they view as a retrospective
    application of new requirements. In particular, the companies objected to our approach
    to assessing spill compliance, especially the use of 20 spills as a threshold for
    investigation. They noted that neither the storm overflows discharge reduction plan
    (SODRP) or the SOAF make reference to a 20 spills standard. They also noted that the 20-
    spill threshold differs from that used by the Environment Agency and that we have not
    previously mentioned the 20 spill standard nor issued any guidance on its application.

16. Thames Water and other water companies have sought to argue that by using a threshold
    of 20 spills as an indicator that spills from storm overflows may be occurring routinely
    and not in exceptional circumstances, that Ofwat has set a new legal standard and that
    this standard is inconsistent with the industry's current approach and with the standard
    that has been applied by the Environment Agency and the Government.

17. Thames Water also argued that our 'novel interpretation' of the UWWTR has been
    imposed without formal consultation or guidance; that it was not invoked in Ofwat’s prior
    investigation of Southern Water; and, that it is at tension with the framework designed to
    discharge water companies' obligations under the UWWTR and in the securing of a
    progressive reduction in storm overflows more generally.

18. Thames Water and other water companies have argued that, rather than use our
    enforcement powers, Ofwat should have consulted with, or issued guidance to, the sector
    on the standard that we expect companies to meet to ensure their compliance with the
    UWWTR. Thames Water has argued, for example, that our failure to do so is inconsistent

                                               on Thames Water

       with our duties under Section 2 WIA91287 which, amongst other things, requires Ofwat to
       have regard to the principles of best regulatory practice. This includes ensuring that our
       regulatory activities are transparent, accountable, proportionate, consistent and
       targeted.

19. Thames Water and the other water companies have also claimed that the industry now
    finds itself in the position that the Government has (through the Environment Agency
    and Defra) established a regulatory baseline (the 60-spill standard under SOAF), which
    we have previously agreed to and endorsed through our price control activities, but is
    now told that it should have been applying a stricter standard that it did not know about
    and could not reasonably have known about.

20. All the water companies have argued that compliance with the UWWTR and the EPR are
    inextricably linked, with the EPR designed and intended to ensure compliance with the
    UWWTR. They claim that by virtue of complying with the Environment Agency's permits
    and by following the SOAF process they are in compliance with the UWWTR, and Ofwat is,
    therefore, incorrect to suggest that companies' obligations under the UWWTR are
    separate from the EPR.

Our response

21. We disagree that we are interpreting the UWWTR in a novel and unprecedented way, or
    that we are seeking to impose a new legal standard. As we explain in Section 2, our
    approach is based on the legislation and relevant caselaw.

22. We agree that the Environment Agency has a duty under Regulation 6(2) UWWTR to
    exercise its permitting functions under the UWWTR in relation to discharges from
    regulated systems so as to limit pollution to receiving waters. However, that duty does not
    supplant or override the obligation owed directly by sewerage undertakers under
    Regulation 4 UWWTR, or Ofwat’s duty to take enforcement action in respect of
    contraventions of that obligation: as Holgate J said in Wildfish at §87, “the EA is not an
    enforcing authority under the WIA 1991 for breaches of the 1994 Regulations”. And in any
    event it is concerned with “the limitation of pollution of receiving waters”, whereas the
    duty in Regulation 4 UWWTR (to ensure, among other things, that treatment plants are
    “designed […], constructed, operated and maintained to ensure sufficient performance
    under all normal local climatic conditions”) is of more general application. The
    companies continue to be directly subject to the obligations under Regulation 4 UWWTR
    notwithstanding the existence of the EPR.

24. Nevertheless, on balance, we think the fact that the companies, erroneously considered

27. To the extent that Thames Water has argued that Ofwat should have sought to first

Ofwat's approach conflicts with companies' legitimate expectations.

29. In its response to our draft decision, Thames Water told us that our approach to the
    enforcement of the UWWTR conflicts with its, and the industry’s, legitimate expectations
    with the EPR and following the SOAF process, that by complying with the EPR and by
    following the SOAF process, it was also complying with the UWWTR and therefore that it

Our response

30. As we explain above, we have based our interpretation of Regulation 4 UWWTR on the
    pre-existing legislation and caselaw dating from 2012 (the subject matter of which
    included Thames Water assets).

The level of Thames Water's non-compliance with Regulation 4 UWWTR
is overstated has not been properly assessed

31. For the reasons outlined above, Thames Water told us that, in its views, it has complied
    with the UWWTR. It also told us that, in any event, in our assessment of whether its sites
    had breached or were in breach of Regulation 4 UWWTR, Ofwat had failed to fully reflect
    the requirements of the UWWTR and SOAF and, as a result, we have likely overstated the
    number of sites in breach and the number of sites included as part of our penalty
    assessment. While we have also addressed many of these points in Sections 3 and 4 of
    this document, we also provide a summary of the main issues raised by Thames Water
    here and our position on those issues.

Ofwat has misinterpreted the scope of the UWWTR

32. Thames Water has argued that the UWWTR is only applicable to agglomerations with a
    population equivalent (PE) of less than 2,000 people and that Ofwat has failed to take the
    necessary step of assessing the extent to which WWTW and storm overflows serve a PE
    equal to or in excess of 2,000.

Our position

33. As acknowledged in Section 2, Regulation 4(2) expressly imposes obligations in respect of
    the provision of collecting systems “for every agglomeration with a population equivalent
    of 2,000 or more”.

34. With respect to Regulation 4(4), Regulation 5 sets minimum treatment requirements
    according to the size of population served by the relevant WWTW. Regulation 5(7)
    explains that, notwithstanding the above, appropriate treatment should be provided for
    all agglomerations.

                                           on Thames Water

35. In relation to our assessment of Thames Water's breaches under Regulation 4(2), as we
    have explained in our draft decision, and again in this final decision, our finding of
    breach relates not to the number of high spilling storm overflows on its network that the
    company failed to deal with as part of the SOAF process, but rather to the company's
    failure to monitor and manage its assets to ensure that it was complying with the UWWTR
    – as evidenced by the fact that in 2022 Thames Water included over 300 network storm
    overflows in its annual EDM return to the Environment Agency. These overflows were
    unmonitored (and so the true scale of spills from Thames Water's network storm
    overflows is likely to have been higher than recorded) and many were also unpermitted.

Ofwat has failed to understand how the BTKNEEC test is applied

36. A number of companies claimed that Ofwat’s position, that they should have conducted
    BTKNEEC assessments for high spilling overflows, runs contrary to previous sectoral
    guidance and, in particular, to the approach used under SOAF. They claim that BTKNEEC
    is an objective standard, with the test being not whether a company has applied
    BTKNEEC but whether, in objective terms, a non-exceptional discharge can be justified
    by cost-benefit analysis that satisfies BTKNEEC.

37. This argument takes two different forms. The first is that Ofwat cannot conclude that
    there has been a breach in respect of a particular site without considering BTKNEEC
    issues. The second is that Ofwat cannot conclude that there has been a breach in
    respect of a particular site unless it concludes on the balance of probabilities that there
    is a BTKNEEC-compliant solution that could be adopted at that site but has not been
    adopted.

Our position

38. Ofwat agrees that a site is only operating in breach of Regulation 4(2) UWWTR if it is both
    high spilling and there is no unimplemented BTKNEEC consistent remedy available to
    improve the position. However, Regulation 4(2) UWWTR also clearly states that companies
    must ensure that they provide collecting systems for the specified agglomerations which
    meet the requirements of Schedule 2 UWWTR including as to the limitation of pollution
    from storm overflows consistent with BTKNEEC. The ECJ made clear that this means that
    storm overflows should only spill in exceptional circumstances unless it would be
    inconsistent with BTKNEEC for those spills to be remedied, and that where BTKNEEC is
    relied upon this should be evidenced and not just asserted. If companies become aware
    that any of their storm overflows are spilling outside exceptional circumstances, their
    obligations under Regulation 4(2) UWWTR therefore require them to ensure that they are
    nevertheless operating consistently with BTKNEEC and to take remedial steps if they are
    not.

Burden of proof and evidence

39. Thames Water also claimed that in our approach to UWWTR, we had improperly reversed
    the burden of proof onto it for evidencing environmental harm, BTKNEEC or exceptional
    circumstance.

Our position

40. Our approach does not reverse the burden of proof with respect to BTKNEEC. Regulation 4
    UWWTR requires the companies to ensure that they comply with BTKNEEC in the way they
    design, construct and maintain their collecting systems in non-exceptional
    circumstances. If there are non-exceptional spills, the companies are also required to
    ensure that they comply with BTKNEEC in considering how to address them.

41. In any event, the companies hold the evidence relevant to their assessment of
    environmental harm and BTKNEEC, which we note they were also required to conduct
    upon reaching the spill thresholds under the SOAF, and we have requested and
    considered evidence held by the companies relating to BTKNEEC as well as environmental
    harm in the course of our investigation.

Our assessment of sites where high spills are due to infiltration

42. In its response to our draft decision, Thames Water also challenged our findings on the
    number of its sites which had spilled more than 60 times due to asset maintenance
    reasons and claimed that we had "likely overstated" the number of its sites that we had
    found to have breached Regulation 4 UWWTR in our penalty assessment. This was
    because we had not taken into account the fact that under SOAF, where the reason for
    the high spills was identified as being due to infiltration (which is categorised under
    asset maintenance), it is recognised that it may take longer than a year to resolve the
    root cause of the spills.

Our position

43. We have considered this point and, as noted in Sections 3 and 4 of this document, we
    sought additional information from Thames Water on the sites where infiltration was
    identified as the reason the site was triggered for investigation under SOAF and on the
    company's plans to address issues at those sites. We have taken this additional evidence
    into account and have revised our assessment of the number of sites we have included as
    part of our penalty assessment. Our updated assessment is explained in Section 4.

                                           on Thames Water

Alleged inconsistency in how remedial actions are treated as part of Ofwat's
assessment of breach of Regulation 4 UWWTR

44. As explained in Section 4, under SOAF where the root cause of a high spill is identified as
    being hydraulic capacity, further investigation is required to assess whether the spill has
    resulted in environmental harm and if a cost beneficial solutions exist to resolve the
    cause of the spill. A failure to carry out further investigation is considered to be a breach
    of Regulation 4 UWWTR. Where no cost beneficial solution is identified or the
    investigation is still ongoing (within reasonable timescales), the site is excluded from
    both the breach assessment and the penalty assessment (as it is not yet known whether
    a cost beneficial solution exists). Where a cost beneficial solution has been identified, the
    site is included in our breach assessment but is excluded from our penalty assessment –
    if these is evidence that cost beneficial solution or remedial action is being implemented
    or will be implemented within a reasonable timescales.

45. In its response to our draft decision, Thames Water welcomed our approach to assessing
    sites where hydraulic capacity was identified as the reason for the high spills under the
    SOAF process but claimed that Ofwat appeared to adopt a different, and inconsistent,
    approach when considering the remedial action that the company was taking, or was
    planning to take, outside of the SOAF process. In particular, it noted that we had not
    adopted the same approach in relation to its remedial work to address FFT, DWF and
    storm tank capacity issues at its 157 "sites of concern" under its Waste Asset Assurance
    Programme (WAAP) or WINEP. In Thames Water's view, these programmes are also steps
    it is taking to ensure its assets are maintained and operated according to BTKNEEC in
    compliance with the UWWTR and therefore, these sites should also be considered not to
    be in breach.

Our response

46. We disagree with Thames Water's claims that we are acting inconsistently in the way in
    which we are treating sites with remediation plans in our breach and penalty
    assessments. We recognise that the companies, wrongly, considered that adherence to
    the SOAF process set the limits of what was required under the UWWTR in relation to
    storm overflows and have taken those regulatory expectations into account when
    assessing penalties. In terms of breach, where a site is spilling outside exceptional
    circumstances, the company is required to assess whether remedial action needs to be
    taken consistent with BTKNEEC. If it is in the process, diligently and expeditiously, of
    carrying out that investigation, it is fulfilling its duty to ensure the operation of its
    network consistent with BTKNEEC.

47. If it transpires that there are improvements that are available consistent with BTKNEEC
    (whether operational, maintenance or improvements to hydraulic capacity), its network
    will not be operating consistently with the UWWTR until those improvements have been
    implemented. Similarly, where hydraulic capacity issues have been identified at a WWTW

                                           on Thames Water

    that require remediation in order for the site to be compliant with the UWWTR and that
    remediation has not been implemented, the site will be non-compliant until that
    remediation has occurred.

The proposed penalty is excessive, unfair and unreasonable, lacks
adequate justification, and is not consistent with past precedent.

48. In its response to our draft decision, Thames Water told us that it does not accept that it
    had breached (and in some cases, is continuing to breach) the UWWTR, section 94 WIA91
    and Condition P of its Licence. On that basis, it argued, that Ofwat’s proposed penalty is
    unfounded, and in any event wholly disproportionate in light of the level of penalties in its
    previous enforcement cases. Similar arguments were also put forward by both Yorkshire
    Water and Northumbrian Water in their responses to their respective draft decisions.

Our position

49. In our draft decision and in our final decision we have set out the evidence that we have
    relied on in our assessment of whether Thames Water has breached UWWTR, section 94
    WIA91 and Condition P of its licence. Given the scale, scope and duration of the issues
    identified during the course of our investigation into Thames Water's management of its
    wastewater treatment assets, we have also explained the reasons why we consider a
    significant penalty is appropriate in this case.

50. In arriving at our penalty assessment, we have followed our published policy statement
    and have sought to adopt a consistent approach across all our investigations. However,
    the level of penalties that Ofwat can impose is a matter of regulatory discretion and
    whilst we have taken account of precedents (including our investigation into Southern
    Water), we are not bound by our previous decisions. Therefore, we assess each of our
    enforcement cases based on the specific circumstances of that case and while the levels
    of penalties in previous cases may provide guidance, they are not determinative of our
    future decisions.

51. Similarly, while Thames Water and other companies have sought to argue that the
    penalty in our current investigations is disproportionate in light of the penalty imposed
    on Southern Water in that case, we again stress that we consider each case individually.

There is a lack of transparency as to how the penalties have been
calculated

52. Thames Water, Yorkshire Water and Northumbrian Water have also claimed that there is
    a lack of transparency as to how the penalties have been calculated and that we have not
    explained adequately how the starting penalty in these decision was reached or how the
    mitigating and aggravating factors have been taken into account.

        Notice of Ofwat’s decision to issue an enforcement order and impose a financial penalty
                                           on Thames Water

Our response

53. Whilst we consider each investigation on a case-by-case basis, and whilst we have
    discretion about the level of penalties to impose, we have also sought to apply our
    published policy consistently across all our investigations.

54. In Section 6 we have explained in detail the factors that we have taken into account in
    arriving at our starting penalty in this case and the reasons for our assessment. We have
    also explained our assessment of all the relevant aggravating and mitigating factors in
    this case.

55. We have additionally provided Thames Water and other companies with an overview of
    the broad framework we have used to guide the decisions we have made on the
    appropriate penalty levels for all the companies that are subject to our wastewater
    investigations. This is included at Appendix A7.


Relevant revenue in the penalty calculation

56. In addition to repeating their arguments that the proposed penalties are excessive,
    disproportionate and inconsistent with those imposed in previous cases, Thames Water
    and a number of other water companies have raised concerns about the revenue streams
    that we have included as "relevant turnover" for the purposes of the penalty assessment.
    For example, Thames Water argued that retail revenue should be excluded from the
    turnover figure, whilst Yorkshire Water considered that revenue associated with
    bioresources should be excluded.

Our response

57. Relevant turnover is determined in accordance with the Water Industry (Determination of
    Turnover for Penalties) Order 2005 (Penalties Order), which in broad terms, defines it as
    revenue from "the provision of goods and services in the course of the [company's]
    regulated activities in respect of which the penalty is imposed". "Regulated activities" of a

62. Some companies (for example, Yorkshire Water and Anglian Water) also argued that

    many of the alleged failures that we identified as part of our investigations can be

Our findings in relation to Thames Water's compliance with section 94 WIA91

67. Thames Water told us that it did not accept that it had breached its duties under section
    94 of the WIA91 and denied that any contravention is ongoing. It claimed that our draft
    decision in this respect relied largely upon a flawed interpretation of the UWWTR and that
    we had failed to substantiate that it had breached section 94 as a stand-alone breach.

68. It argued that Ofwat is required, as set out in the 2019 Southern Water penalty decision,
    to assess whether there has been systemic failure with the company’s obligations and
    whether Thames Water's actions were the actions to be expected of a reasonable
    company. In its view, we have not considered adequately whether Thames Water failed to
    act reasonably in the circumstances and have, therefore, in its view, failed to meet the
    legal test for a finding of breach under section 94 WIA91.

69. Thames Water claimed that it had, in fact, acted reasonably in the circumstances
    according to best industry standards and in the absence of any guidance from Ofwat on
    how it proposed to interpret and enforce Regulation 4 of the UWWTR. It also claimed that
    it had relied on its legitimate expectation that compliance with the EPR and SODRP
    would mean compliance with the UWWTR and had sought funding under the various

Our response

  70. We disagree that our interpretation or the UWWTR is flawed for the reasons explained
      previously. We have also addressed the point about companies' legitimate expectations
      above.

  71. As explained in our draft decision document and as set out again in Section 2 of this final
      decision document, each breach of Regulation 4 UWWTR itself constitutes a breach of
      section 94 WIA91. We have applied the appropriate legal test in our findings relating to
      breach of section 94 WIA91.

  72. In reaching our findings in relation to the extent to which the company has complied,
      and continues to comply with, its obligations under section 94, we have based our
      assessment on the magnitude and extent of Thames Water's failures under the UWWTR
      which point to a systemic failure to make appropriate provision for effectually dealing
      with the contents of sewers and constitutes an ongoing breach of section 94 WIA91. In
      reaching our findings, we have considered the actions that a reasonable company would
      take.

  Our findings in relation to Thames Water's compliance with Condition P

  73. In its response to our draft decision Thames Water told us that it had carefully considered
      Ofwat’s draft decision and whilst it accepted that its governance processes could have
      been better, it did not accept that these fell below the standards required by Condition P
      such that it had breached Condition P historically, nor did it accept that any such breach
      is ongoing.

  74. In respect of our finding of historic breach of Condition P, Thames Water denied any
      intimation that it had failed to spend appropriately on compliance or that it had
      improperly preferred areas of the business which were subject to greater regulatory
      scrutiny. It noted that whilst its Board must make challenging decisions on compliance,
      it had spent all of its PR14 allowance in relation to its wastewater activities in AMP6 and
      was expected to have overspent relative to its PR19 allowance for AMP7.

  75. Thames Water also rejected any suggestion that it should have met any alleged
      compliance funding gap within AMP6 and AMP7 with shareholder funds or could have
      realistically secured more in-AMP funding from Ofwat within this period. It pointed to the
      fact that its shareholders had already injected significant new equity into the business
      and had received no external dividend for many years. It again reiterated its view that the
      regulatory standard included in the draft decision represents a new legal standard which

                                           on Thames Water

    Thames Water and its shareholders were not aware of and could not expected to bear
    retrospectively.

76. In relation to any continuing breach, it pointed to the enhancements it had made as part
    of its Turnaround Plan and the changes to its governance processes to improve its
    resources and systems of planning and internal control, including the advances in
    monitoring and data assessment, institutionalised training and cultural programmes and
    enhanced governance processes. These changes, in Thames Water's view, indicated that
    even if the company had breached Condition P in the past, there is no ongoing breach.

Our response

77. Under licence Condition P, companies are required to ensure that they have the
    necessary processes in place to enable them to meet all their regulatory obligations and
    to assure Ofwat annually that they have sufficient resources to enable them to do so.

78. Based on the evidence that we have seen, we have concluded that, from at least March
    2017, Thames Water failed to act in the manner best calculated to ensure it had adequate
    financial and management resources and systems of planning and internal control in
    place to carry out its regulated activities, and in particular to manage and effectively
    operate its WWTW and networks to meet their environmental obligations under their
    permits, the UWWTR and section 94 WIA91.

79. As explained in our draft decision and again in this final decision document, we would
    have expected a company to have in place adequate systems and controls in order to
    prevent, identify and address the issues of the type outlined in this case. As we also
    explained it is clear from the company's own compliance risk assessments that that the
    company was aware that it had significant compliance risks across numerous sites and
    yet, did not respond with any real urgency to address them. These risks related not to any
    new standard that Thames Water alleges that Ofwat is now seeking to enforce (and which
    it therefore could not be expected to have complied with), but rather a failure to comply
    with its existing environmental permits.

80. We therefore remain of the view that Thames Water neglected its obligations in this case.
    The Board of Thames Water placed reliance on a variety of teams and systems to
    understand the performance of its WWTW and networks. These systems and processes
    were ineffective and focused on a relatively narrow set of indicators or parameters which
    fed into the company's EPA report or were relevant to the company's PCs and ODIs. As a
    result, the Board did not seek sufficient information to adequately assure itself, or Ofwat
    via its annual certificate, as to the company's full compliance position, nor to sufficiently
    scrutinise performance in order to drive improvements and secure compliance.

81. Thames Water has challenged our assessment that its management team and Board did
    not receive, nor seek, sufficient information and assurance on the operational

        Notice of Ofwat’s decision to issue an enforcement order and impose a financial penalty
                                           on Thames Water

    performance of the company’s wastewater assets and their compliance with relevant
    legal obligations. It also rejected any suggestion that it had improperly assured Ofwat in
    relation to the adequacy of its resources and systems of planning and internal control in
    its RFC and its RCS. In its view, the company has, at all time, followed Ofwat guidance in
    relation to the preparation of the RFC and has made suitable disclosures – including
    disclosures relating to permit compliance in its RFC for 2021 -2022 and 2022-23.

82. We have set out the evidence we have relied on in reaching our findings in relation to
    Thames Water's compliance with Condition P in Sections 3 and 4. This evidence is drawn
    mainly from Thames Water's Board papers and minutes and, in our assessment, indicates
    that, until relatively recently, the focus of the management team and Board was on
    metrics relevant to the Environment Agency's EPA and the company's PCs and ODIs under
    the price control and not on its wider regulatory obligations. Despite Thames Water's
    challenge, our findings in relation to the limited nature of the information being
    presented to, and discussed by Board, also mirrors the findings of the company's own
    internal audit reports which also highlighted the risks arising from the company's narrow
    focus on a limited number of performance indicators and metrics.

83. Similarly, in relation to Thames Water's RFCs, while we recognise that the company has
    now taken steps to report on risks associated with its wider regulatory obligations, it only
    began to do so for the 2021-22 RFC – which post-dates the opening of our investigation.
    Prior to that, and despite the compliance risks which had been identified under the
    company's G2G programme, these were not referred to in earlier RFCs.

84. We welcome the steps that Thames Water has taken/is taking to improve its processes,
    oversight and governance. However, the fact that the company considers that these
    changes are needed also serves to underline the fact that there were deficiencies in its
    previous processes and systems. It is also too early to conclude with any degree of
    confidence that the changes that Thames Water has now put in place are sufficient to
    enable us to conclude that there is no ongoing breach of Condition P. This is because of
    the fact that the company appears to be still uncovering new potential issues and its
    understanding of the steps that it needs to take, and the investment that this will
    require, is still evolving.

85. Finally, in relation to Thames Water's challenge that as it spent all the funds it was
    allocated for its wastewater activities under the price review process in AMP6 and is
    expected to have overspent in AMP7, that it had acted as a reasonable company within
    the confines of the price review process and the need to balance competing priorities
    with a limited budget. We disagree. As explained in our draft decision and as repeated in
    this final decision, it is our assessment that Thames Water failed to act with sufficient
    urgency to address known compliance risks across its wastewater network, that is, it
    failed to act to ensure its compliance with its existing environmental permit conditions.
    Companies, including Thames Water, were funded to meet these permit conditions as
    part of the price review process and also assured us annually that they had sufficient

      resources to enable them to do so. Despite this, during the course of our investigation,
      Thames Water identified 157 sites, or two thirds of its sites with permits or TDCs, which
      had failed to meet their FFT permit conditions. Many of its sites were also potentially non-
      compliant in relation to DWF and storm tank capacity. Moreover, Thames Water has
      claimed that had it requested additional funds to enable it to address known compliance
      issues more rapidly, the likelihood is that Ofwat would have rejected that request.
      Leaving aside this unsubstantiated assertion, Thames Water itself has admitted that its
      previous business plans and funding were based upon meeting compliance with existing
      permits. Moreover, even when opportunities did arise for companies to access additional
      investment, for example via the Green Recovery Programme and Accelerated
      Infrastructure Delivery Project, Thames Water failed to take advantage of them. In our
      view, this indicates a failure by the company to prioritise spending on compliance with
      the full range of its legal and regulatory obligations. While Thames Water has challenged
      our assessment, again, these issues and risks had been flagged by its own internal
      reports and reviews – and yet it failed to act. In the 2019 review of the company's
      compliance regime, which was undertaken following the publication of our findings in
      the Southern Water case, for example, it noted that "the governance behind capital
      spend and investment should formally consider and prioritise compliance requirements
      moving forward". This recommendation was in turn based on the fact that "compliance
      risks and resilience for all aspects of permits were not considered as a high priority in
      decisions on capital investment spend and suggested that, in order to mitigate these
      risks, the company's approach to risk prioritisation should be considered; that
      compliance issues should be ranked higher; and that awareness of all compliance
      obligations should be increased".

Fines should be used to remedy problems in the areas affected by the

87. A number of respondents 291 called for any fines imposed to be used for the benefit of the

    respondent (generally based on their local interests), but a common theme was that the
